https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Looped Oxide Catalysis: The Prospect of Bio Oil Deoxygenation over Reduced Metal Oxides
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: One of the key challenges in the production of liquid transportation fuels from cellulosic biomass is the upgrading of primary bioliquids to reduce the total oxygen content. This upgrading step is necessary to generate fuels with higher combustion energy, volatility and thermal stability and lower viscosity and molecular weight. Hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) of biomass fast-pyrolysis and liquefaction bio-oils with renewably-sourced H 2 represents a promising carbon-neutral upgrading pathway. However, HDO processing is limited by requisite high pressures and by the destruction of chemical exergy during the reaction of H­ 2 with easily-reduced oxygenate compounds. As an alternative to HDO, we propose a two-step thermochemical cycle wherein a metal oxide is reduced to its metal or to a lower-valence oxide in a high-temperature solar furnace and subsequently reacted with a bio-oil feedstock, reforming the higher oxide and yielding a deoxygenated fuel product. This process, which we have termed “looped oxide catalysis” (LOC), synthesizes concepts from the fields of solar thermochemical hydrogen production, chemical looping, and hydroprocessing and may allow for low-pressure deoxygenation of bio-oil while also achieving high exergy efficiency. From a set of eighty possible LOC catalysts we have identified five most-promising candidates on the basis of known diffusion kinetics, catalytic activity in HDO reactions, and metal-oxygen bond strength. Oxides with low metal-oxygen bond strength will be unable to abstract oxygen from bio-oil oxygenates, while oxides with high metal-oxygen bond strength will require excess energy to reduce. Therefore oxides with intermediate metal-oxygen bond strength are most desirable; this behavior is illustrated in a thermodynamic “volcano plot.” An exergy analysis of the LOC cycle is developed for the five candidate oxides to identify inherent thermodynamic irreversibilities. Additionally, the experimental performance of the five candidate LOC catalysts in a continuous-flow reactor will be discussed in comparison with traditional HDO catalysts.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Effect of Promoter Deposition Order on Platinum-, Ruthenium-, and Rhenium-Promoted Cobalt Fischer-Tropsch Catalysts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Abstract The effects of noble metal (NM) promoter (Pt, Re, or Ru) deposition order were investigated in commercially-representative Co Fischer-Tropsch catalysts (nominally 25 wt% Co on a La stabilized alumina support). The effects of deposition sequence (co-deposition vs. sequential deposition) were studied in terms of NM retention and distribution, Co crystallite size, Co reducibility, and catalyst activity and selectivity. Ru retention was <48% with more severe losses for co-deposition (85% loss). Sequentially deposited Co/Ru showed poor Ru distribution, unlike co-deposited Co/Ru. Excellent retention and uniform distribution were observed for both Pt and Re promoted catalysts. Cobalt crystallite sizes were smaller for all three co-deposited catalysts (~4.2 nm for all NMs) when compared to any of the sequentially deposited catalysts. Although sequentially deposited catalysts required higher reduction temperatures (TPR), they had greater extents of reduction (EORs) relative to co-deposited catalysts. CO depletion rates and turnover frequencies (TOFs) for co-deposited Co/Pt and Co/Re were 2-3 times higher than their sequentially deposited counterparts. Methane selectivities were lower for co-deposited Co/Pt and Co/Re. It is interesting to note that the smaller Co crystallite sizes (co-deposition) resulted in more active catalysts than those with larger crystallites (sequentially deposition), which is counter to previous work on unpromoted Co catalysts. The co-deposited Co/Pt catalyst was found to be statistically more active than the unpromoted Co catalyst, while the corresponding sequentially deposited catalyst was less active. Overall, co-deposited Co/Pt and Co/Re catalysts showed superior catalytic performance by all standards of judgment when compared to their sequentially deposited counterparts.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: The Oxygen Reduction Reaction on Nitrogen-Doped Graphene: A Density Functional Theory Study
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Increased global awareness of negative implications associated with climate change fuels the search for more sustainable forms of energy generation. Fuel cells have received considerable attention due to their efficiency, reliability, and lack of emissions. However, the sluggish kinetics of the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) remains one of the main limitations. Furthermore, current ORR catalysts use platinum, which requires a sizeable economic investment due to the high cost. Experimental work shows nitrogen-doped graphene (CN x ) catalysts operate at an overpotential similar to that of commercial platinum catalysts, but an atomic level understanding of the source of activity in these materials is still lacking. This first principles study utilizes density functional theory to model the elementary steps of the ORR on CN x materials to understand the structure-activity relationship of these materials. This study explicitly includes the role of water through inclusion of an ice-like water layer. We will discuss the impact of water on the derived overpotential of the ORR on CN x for comparison to previous work on the Pt(111). A first principles understanding of nitrogen-doped graphene activity in appropriately modeled environments will be important in efforts to improve the performance of CN x materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Control of Furfural Hydrogenation Selectivity Via Modified Ni-Based Catalysts Using Self-Assembled Monolayers
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: In a world of rising technology and limited fuel sources, the research and production of biofuels is of utmost importance. Furfural, a common component of bio-oil, is a platform chemical with the potential to create a variety of products, including an important fuel additive, methylfuran. A nickel catalyst, unlike the commonly used copper and palladium, is of interest due to its low cost despite its high reactivity and low selectivity of methylfuran. We believe that specific adsorption of furfural onto the catalyst determines its preferred reaction pathway and primary products. By adding a dense self-assembled monolayer (SAM) to the nickel catalyst surface, we can control furfural adsorption geometry, which in turn affects reaction selectivity. Experiments utilized three primary thiols: adamantanethiol (AT), octadecanethiol (C18), and 1,2-benzenedithiol (Benz). We found that benzenedithiol improved methylfuran selectivity from 10% to 88% on the pure nickel catalyst. The uncoated NiCu bimetallics decreased the selectivity of furan but did not demonstrate complete hydrodeoxygenation to methylfuran, resulting in production of furfuryl alcohol. The SAM coated bimetallics eliminated furfuryl alcohol as a product by allowing further reaction of the furfuryl alcohol to methylfuran.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Quantification of Hydrogen and Oxygen Production to Assess Selectivity of Electrocatalysts for Solar Water Splitting
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Photoelectrochemical water splitting presents an environmentally friendly means of producing hydrogen for use as fuel or industrial feedstock; current research in this field primarily focuses on developing the ideal catalysts and semiconductors for this process. It is undesirable for a given electrocatalyst/semiconductor pair to have less than 100% faradaic efficiency for the solar water splitting reaction, which literature has shown may occur through unwanted side reactions or catalyst/semiconductor degradation. A technique is developed to quantify the production of hydrogen and oxygen in a photoelectrochemical cell in order to assess the faradaic efficiency of electrocatalysts and semiconductor absorbers used for solar water splitting. The process involves commercial hydrogen and oxygen microsensor probes and a custom photoelectrochemical cell optimized for accurate product quantification. The airtight cell consists of two identical compartments separated by an ion exchange membrane and is equipped with ports for all necessary electrodes, product detection sensors, a gas purge, and a thermocouple. Three-point calibrations are performed prior to experimentation using an inert gas purge and then injecting known volumes of hydrogen or oxygen into the cell. The technique’s accuracy is confirmed by ensuring measurements of approximately 100% faradaic efficiency for platinum and iridium electrodes for the hydrogen evolution reaction and oxygen evolution reaction, respectively (a baseline based on previous studies from the literature). The accuracy of hydrogen measurements is further confirmed using gas chromatography. Initial applications include assessing crystalline molybdenum disulfide catalysts on n + silicon wafer cathodes, which are measured to have a faradaic efficiency of 98.6%. Future work will initially focus on improving the technique’s precision and determining the effect of changing temperature on the sensors’ accuracy, after which additional catalysts and semiconductors will be evaluated, including tantalum nitride and strontium titanate photoanodes.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Kinetic Analysis of Aqueous-Phase Pd-Catalyzed, Cu-Free Direct Arylation of Terminal Alkynes Using a Hydrophilic Ligand
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The engineering of reaction mixtures that ensure the solubility of inorganic salt byproducts without compromising the reactivity is a grand challenge for continuous flow manufacturing in upstream pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals process development. Aqueous cross-coupling reactions are possible solutions. We report the study of an aqueous phase Pd-catalyzed Cu-free direct arylation of an alkyne using a hydrophilic ligand towards understanding the role of water on the cross-coupling kinetics. Kinetic analyses of theoretically estimated molar flux rates and the measured reaction kinetics reveal a transition from mass transfer to kinetically controlled deprotonation and carbopalladation mechanisms. Interfacial contact areas of immiscible aqueous–organic phases control the crossover from the mass-transfer-limited to the reaction-rate-limited regime. Highly agitated batch reactors and multiphase capillary flow reactors are needed to overcome the mass transport limitations and, thus, discover the transition from the apparent reaction kinetics to the true reaction kinetics. Comparison of previously reported Density Functional Theory calculations with experimentally measured activation energies, ranging from 14.8 to 20.0 kcal/mol, elucidates the theoretical possibility of designing the aqueous phase C–C cross-coupling reaction with similar reactivity as purely organic reactions. Although ambiguity remains concerning which reaction step is rate-determining in either the deprotonation or the carbopalladation mechanism, our discovery undergirds that one mechanism or the other could dominate in aqueous designed direct arylations.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Hydrogen Production from Solar Water Splitting
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: H 2 Production from Solar Water Splitting Faidy Rusinque Mentor: Xianqin Wang New Jersey Institute of Technology Newark, NJ Abstract: In the last few years there has been an intensive research focused on alternative H 2 production technologies. Solar to-Hydrogen conversion methods such as photocatalytic water splitting need to be developed so that the transition to a hydrogen-based energy infrastructure can be made effortlessly. Producing hydrogen from water with tunable band gap of TiO 2 will resolve several issues: Proper utilization of the solar energy spectrum, clean hydrogen production, and minimization of CO 2 emissions. TiO 2 is perhaps the most promising semiconductor material due to its effectiveness for harnessing solar energy for H 2 generation. In this study we determined H 2 production activities over a series of TiO 2 -based catalysts from solar water splitting. We investigated the correlation between TiO 2 properties with the hydrogen production activities by tuning particle size, TiO 2 surface areas, and different metal (Pt) loading on TiO 2 . TiO 2 -based catalysts were synthesized with incipient impregnation method and characterized with CO chemisorption, temperature programmed reduction and desorption, surface area measurements at liquid nitrogen temperature, powder XRD patterns, and activity measurements. The activity results showed that the TiO 2 surface area, metal dispersion and particle size affect the H 2 Production rate.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Catalytic Conversion of Landfill Gas to Liquid Fuel
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Landfill gas can be captured, converted, and used as an energy source. Approximately 234 MM tons/year of municipal solid waste is produced in United States, with the average landfill collecting 2800 ft 3 /min of landfill gas (LFG). Most of this gas is wasted by flaring while landfills spend $8,000 per day on diesel fuel for its vehicle fleet. The process involves two specialized catalysts, Ni-Mg supported on Ce 0.6 Zr 0.4 O 2 for use in a Tri-reforming reactor, turning CO 2 and methane into hydrogen and carbon monoxide (syngas). This syngas is converted using a silica eggshell catalyst in the Fischer-Tropsch reactor (FTSR). Using both the tri-reforming and the FTS reactors in tandem enables conversion of the landfill gas directly into a tailored fuel cut of middle distillates (diesel and jet fuel) without creating heavier hydrocarbons. The catalysts combat current issues of coke formation and lowers the cost of synthetic fossil fuels. The downscaling of extremely large FTS reactors is important to the implementation of this system on a wider scale. Current efforts are aimed at integration of the reactors and scaling of the prototype system.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Composition-Activity Correlation of Gold-Supported Nickel Cobalt Cerium Catalyst for Electrochemical Oxygen Evolution
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Inspired by natural photosynthesis, artificial photosynthesis is a promising renewable energy technology that produces valuable fuel from water, carbon dioxide and sunlight with no CO 2 emissions. The competence of this technology depends heavily on the catalysts for oxygen evolution reaction (OER). The catalysts must have a low overpotential, consist of earth-abundant materials, and be durable to corrosion. We now report the superior performance and stability of novel Ni-Co-Ce ternary heterogeneous catalyst electrodeposited on gold substrate. Activity versus correlation study of Ni-Co-Ce has been conducted using various electrochemistry techniques and Inductive Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS). All electrochemical studies were done in 1.0M KOH at room temperature. Activity studies showed that certain compositions of Ni-Co-Ce catalysts demonstrated overpotentials as low as 270mV. In addition to its high catalytic efficiency, stable performance for over two hours was demonstrated through stability tests. ICP-MS tests verified the actual catalyst film composition, as opposed to electrolyte composition, and revealed that the activity depends closely with Ce composition. This study establishes the basis for further mechanistic studies and scale up of artificial photosynthesis technology.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Kinetics of 2,3-Butanediol Reaction with Cu-ZSM-5 (23)
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The rising costs and harmful environmental impacts of fossil fuels has made developing renewable energies very important. Through bacterial fermentation, biomass can be converted into 2 ,3 -butanediol (2,3-BDO). Using a bifunctional catalyst to catalyze both a hydrogenation and dehydration reaction, 2 ,3 -BDO can be converted in butene, which can then be used as a jet additive. In this study, the kinetics of the 2 ,3 -BDO reaction with catalyst Cu-ZSM-5 (23) was investigated using a small-scale batch reactor. The reaction was run at various reaction times, temperatures, and with or without hydrogen gas present. The liquid products were analyzed using a gas chromatography mass spectrometer. The gas phase was studied using a thermal conductivity detector and flame ionization detector. By identifying the types and amounts of products made, a new reaction mechanism was proposed for the conversion of 2 ,3 -butanediol into butene. This mechanism is shown in Figure 1. The butadiene pathway seemed to be favored over the pathway involving the formation of propanol. Hydrogen was seen as a byproduct of the reaction. More tests should be done on this reaction to further modify the mechanism. Determining an accurate reaction mechanism is important to designing a catalyst that will best optimize the production of butene and make its production cost competitive with petroleum based butene. Figure 1. Proposed mechanism of 2 ,3 -butanediol conversion to butene using Cu-ZSM-5 (23) catalyst.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: New Solid Acid Catalyst for Brown Grease Biodiesel Production
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: There is a big movement in our country to turn many of our processes more sustainable and environmentally friendly. Alternative fuels have started to play a role in this, with ethanol and biodiesel being added to regular petroleum based gasses to help decrease their environmental impact. Biodiesel is created when fats and other carbon chains are reacted with small chained alcohols. Biodiesel is currently made from various vegetable oils and “yellow grease”, used kitchen oils that contain slight amounts of fatty acids, but still easily converted to biodiesel. But another form of grease, brown grease, can also be used to make biodiesel. Brown grease commonly refers to sewer and water treatment waste that contains 50-100% FFA (free fatty acids). Currently brown grease is disposed of by dumping it in landfills or incinerating it. Neither of the methods are particularly environmentally friendly since the heavy metals trapped in the grease either leak into the land or get released into the air when incinerated. But if the oil layers of brown grease were to be converted into biodiesel, the stress the waste causes on our environment would lessen and a usable resource would be created. Brown grease cannot be prepared in the same way as vegetable oils and “yellow grease” due to the high content of FFA. When triglyceride rich oils are converted a base catalyst is used as transesterification happens quicker in the presence of a base then in the presence of an acid. But if FFA is reacted in the presence of a base, any ions or impurities in the brown grease will cause saponification instead of esterification, and soap instead of biodiesel will be created. So esterification is generally done with an acid as a catalyst. The most common catalysts for esterification are the readily available hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid. Both of the acids are liquids and get washed away when the biodiesel is cleaned with water, so each time new catalyst must be used. A solid acid catalyst theoretically would be able to catalyze the reaction and be reusable through several reactions since it can be easily separated and retained. A new acid catalyst (OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H]) was made from the self-assembly of resol precursors, hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) cross-linker, and a tri-block copolymer template of Pluronic® F127 (Sigma-Aldrich) (Scheme 1). This created the OMR-[HMTA] backbone which when reacted with 1,4-butanesultone, forms OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H]. This catalyst was made in lab to compare to the commercially available Amberlyst 15 solid acid and the commonly used non-reusable hydrochloric acid. When the physical proportions of our catalyst was compared to that of the Amberlyst 15, the OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H] had a larger BET surface area and a larger pore volume. This would suggest that it would be better for reacting with more of the catalyst being available to use per mass. Two treatments of the brown grease were tested to compare the catalysts. The first process starts with 20 mL of brown grease that is reacted with excess methanol and 5% weight with respect to oil of catalyst at 65°C until there was under 1% FFA by looking at the acid number found using a 0.07 M potassium hydroxide titration using ASTM Method D6751. After the first reaction, the sample was centrifuged to separate any solid catalyst from the oil/biodiesel sample, and then the sample was washed with distilled water then dried by bubbling air through it. The sample was then put into a new reactor with excess methanol and 5% (w/w) of KOH at 65°C for one hour to convert the glyceride portions of the grease to biodiesel. The second way to treat the sample was to try and have esterification and transesterification happen in one step. 10 g of brown grease oil was reacted with a methanol and the acid catalysts for 5 hours at 65°C. The methanol/oil had about a 40:1 molar ratio (excess), and the catalyst/oil mass ratio was .05:1. Each catalyst was tested under the same conditions above, and for just esterification, the OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H] ended up converting about 99.5% of the FFA to biodiesel after only 1.5 hours. Both Amberlyst 15 and HCl on the other hand had less than a 98% conversion of FFA after 8 hours. When the one step esterification and transesterification was done, OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H] ended up converting about 75% of the triglycerides to biodiesel after 5 hours, which ended up being the equilibrium. The other catalysts ended up converting less than 65% of the triglycerides after a 5 hour period. While the triglyceride conversion was very good for an acid catalyzed transesterification, the final biodiesel just missed passing the ASTM D 6751 specifications because of a too high level of total glycerin in the fuel. The mesporous solid acid catalyst proved to be extremely reactive for the esterification of FFA in brown grease, and when transesterification was done with KOH after the final biodiesel product passed all ASTM quality checks.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Adsorption Studies of Biomass-Derived Molecules in HY and NaY Zeolites By Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics Calculations
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: An embedded-cluster model and Density Functional Theory (DFT) are employed to investigate the adsorption energy of unsaturated aliphatic, aromatic and heterocyclic compounds in HY and NaY zeolites. The quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) ONIOM method is used to model the catalytically active site and the surrounding zeolitic environment, and the results are calculated using the Gaussian 09 computational package and compared to those calculated by Nikbin et al. 1 using a quantum cluster. Our results show that 1) ethylene exhibits the weakest binding among all adsorbates considered in both zeolites, regardless of the cluster models and basis sets employed; 2) in HY zeolite, the quantum cluster calculations predict comparable binding energies of oxa-norbornene and p-xylene, while the QM/MM calculations predict significantly higher binding energy of oxa-norbornene than that of p-xylene; 3) in NaY zeolite, both the quantum cluster and the ONIOM scheme predict very similar binding energies of oxa-norbornene and p-xylene, regardless of the cluster models and basis sets used; 4) smaller clusters tend to underestimate the binding energy; 5) the QM/MM methodology is very sensitive to the choice of cluster size and basis set, as the use of different cluster models and basis sets can contribute to differences of more than 7 kcal/mol and 5 kcal/mol in binding energy, respectively; 6) the parallel configuration of ethylene and DMF co-adsorption in HY zeolite was found to have much higher adsorption energy than the vertical configuration. Reference 1. Nikbin, N.; Caratzoulas, S.; Vlachos, D. G. (submitted to J. Catal)

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Multi-Enzyme Colocalization on Nanocarriers for Investigating Biosynthesis
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Many cascaded biological reactions are catalyzed by enzymes that exist as multi-enzyme complexes. The spatial colocalization of enzymes in these complexes increases the reaction efficiency by ensuring that the reactive intermediates have rapid access to neighboring active sites and maintaining high local concentrations. Although some work has been done on colocalizing model enzymes, there is a lack of knowledge regarding less robust enzymes. Inspired by nature, we immobilized and colocalized two diterpene synthases (DTS) that catalyze the production of sclareol, a valuable fragrance prized in the perfume industry, onto polymeric and nonpolymeric nanoparticles (NPs). Colocalization of DTS enzymes onto NPs can increase the reaction efficiency by producing local environments that facilitate the catalysis of sclareol. The immobilization of these enzymes onto a NP can also improve their stability. Our strategy for immobilization was designed for the binding of histidine-tagged enzymes on to nickel nitrilotriacetic acid-functionalized NPs. We investigated the binding efficiency and retained catalytic activity of the enzyme-nanoparticle conjugates for silica NPs (SiNPs), polystyrene NPs, and gold NPs. We achieved significant binding for SiNPs, but there was little retained catalytic activity (1.1%). Polystyrene NPs also bound a substantial amount of enzymes, but sclareol production could not be determined because these NPs interfered with our hexane extraction process. Gold nanoparticles did not disrupt the activity of the enzyme, but the high cost of this material made it prohibitively expensive to procure quantities that would load a substantial amount of enzymes. An ideal nanocarrier will be one that yields a high binding capacity while retaining the catalytic activity of the loaded enzymes and should be amenable to quantitative assays and extractions.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Alcohol Dehydration over Zr-KIT-6: Lewis Acidic Zr-Incorporated Mesoporous Silicates
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Dehydration of alcohols over a solid acid catalyst is a key step in producing alkenes from bioalcohols obtained by fermentation and C-C coupling using either Guerbet synthesis or hydroformylation. The common solid acid catalysts used for dehydration in industry are zeolites [1]. However, their microporous structure induces pore diffusion limitations with either progressively longer chain alcohols or sugar alcohols such as glycerol, rendering them susceptible to deactivation by fouling [2]. MCM-type zeolites with a mesoporous structure have been attempted to address this problem [3], but low hydrothermal stability and structural reproducibility are significant drawbacks [4]. To address these disadvantages, we have developed a solid Lewis acidic catalyst with a tunable pore size by incorporating Zr into the mesoporous silicate structure KIT-6. Characterization of the catalyst shows a narrow pore size distribution (with mean pore size ~7 nm) with a high number of medium-strength acid sites depending on Zr content [4]. Zr-KIT-6 has been tested for dehydration of linear C 2 -C 4 alcohols. In the 190-300 °C temperature range, the Zr-KIT-6 catalysts showed > 98% selectivity to propene. The intrinsic rate constants obtained in the absence of mass transfer limitations scale with the number of acid sites in the various Zr-KIT-6 samples. The intrinsic activation energy was ~49 kJ/mol and the catalyst activity was stable for several days during continuous runs in a fixed-bed reactor [5]. These results along with those from the dehydration of other alcohols such as ethanol will be presented. References 1. Tanabe, K., Hölderich, W.F., 1999. Industrial application of solid acid–base catalysts. Applied Catalysis A: General 181, 399–434. 2. Wilson, K., Clark, J.H., 2000. Solid acids and their use as environmentally friendly catalysts in organic synthesis. Pure and Applied Chemistry 72, 1313–1319. 3. Haishi, T., Kasai, K., Iwamoto, M., 2011. Fast and Quantitative Dehydration of Lower Alcohols to Corresponding Olefins on Mesoporous Silica Catalyst. Chemistry Letters 40, 614–616. 4. Ramanathan, A., Subramaniam, B., Maheswari, R., Hanefeld, U., 2013. Synthesis and characterization of Zirconium incorporated ultra large pore mesoporous silicate, Zr–KIT-6. Microporous and Mesoporous Materials 167, 207–212. 5. Pan, Q., Ramanathan, A., Snavely, W.K., Chaudhari, R.V., Subramaniam, B., 2013. Synthesis and Dehydration Activity of Novel Lewis Acidic Ordered Mesoporous Silicate: Zr-KIT-6. Ind. Eng. Chem. Res.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: The Effect of Co-Solvent & Ordered Lattice Structure on Catalysis of Biodiesel Production in Microreactors
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: In this study, microreactors are used to make fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel). Microreactors have many advantages over traditional reaction systems due to scale. Benefits include an increase in product purity and a reduction of processing time from hours to seconds. Microfluidic channel size is 50 µm by 500 µm with length of 3 to 15 cm. The channels are coated with a metal base catalyst, Nickel (II) Oxide. This metal catalyst converts a wide variety of vegetable oils to biodiesel. Also, typical feedstock impurities, such as free fatty acids, are successfully converted to biodiesel. Variations in temperature, feedstock composition, and the multiphase nature of the feedstock are also being investigated. Microreactors, in this study, have already successfully produced levels of conversion equivalent to stirred tank systems while reducing hours of processing time to minutes. Additionally, adding free fatty acid to the SBO/methanol feed as a co-solvent, reducing processing fluid to a single phase, has already increased initial global rates. Currently, further design improvements, such as increased catalyst surface coverage and the introduction of ordered lattice structures, are being employed in order to reduce processing time to seconds.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: The Effect Of InVO 4 Coupling On The Photocatalytic Activity Of Anatase and Mixed Phase TiO 2 For Organic Decomposition
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: To increase sustainability of water systems, focus must be turned to the removal of persistent contaminants, including dyes, pesticides, and cyanobacterial metabolites. Photocatalysis, an Advanced Oxidation Process, has greater potential for treating persistent organic contaminants than traditional methods such as chlorine and potassium permanganate. TiO 2 is an effective, inexpensive, and stable photocatalyst used for the decomposition of organics, however; it is limited by its band gap (3.0-3.2 eV) which primarily absorbs in the ultraviolet portion of the spectrum. This project is innovative because it will use the indium vanadate semiconductor, InVO 4 , alloyed to TiO 2 , to increase visible range photoactivity. TiO 2 occurs in several crystalline phases (e.g. anatase, rutile, and brookite).The objective of this study was to determine if the effect on photoactivity of InVO 4 alloying was consistent for pure phase and mixed phase TiO 2 . Pure anatase and mixed phase TiO 2­ (Degussa P25) were used. Batch reactions were carried out at atmospheric pressure and ambient temperature in 1-L pyrex reactors stirred at 250 rpm. The light source was “Daylight Spectrum” florescent bulbs. Photocatalytic activity was determined by monitoring methyl orange concentration using UV-Vis analysis at 15 min intervals. From the data collected, the effect of InVO 4 coupling on the photoactivity was not consistent between anatase and P25 TiO 2­ . Decomposition by the anatase composite was retarded, but decomposition by the mixed phase composite was enhanced. Although these results were unexpected, current research implicates decomposition may occur via two different mechanisms, which may explain why the coupling of InVO 4 affected the phases differently.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Controlled nucleation and overgrowth of platinum on silver nanoparticles Traditional catalytic processes are primarily driven by thermal energy derived from fossil fuels, which is not sustainable or energy efficient. An alternative option would be to captivate the energy released from the sun. The conversion of solar energy to chemical energy is an uprising innovation to drive selective chemical processes. The storage of energy in chemical bonds through visible light positively leads to the remission of pollution and overcomes many of the limitations of fossil fuels. Metallic nanoparticles, which exhibit a unique interaction with visible light, can be synthesized with different geometries and optimized optical properties. In this work, we show that bimetallic nanoparticles with engineered photocatalytic and optical properties can be optimized through the control of nanoparticle geometry, rates of metal precursor addition, concentration of reducing agents, and weight loading. These bimetallic nanostructures will be tested for thermal and photothermal reactivity to show that they can be utilized for the efficient conversion of solar energy into chemical bonds.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: An Operando Molecular Spectroscopic and DFT Calculation Investigation of Methane Aromatization By Supported Mo/ZSM-5 Catalysts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: An Operando Molecular Spectroscopic and DFT Calculation Investigation of Methane Aromatization by Supported Mo/ZSM-5 Catalysts The recent discovery of abundant shell gas has renewed interest in conversion of gas to liquids technology (GTL). The GTL technology has the potential to convert a significant percentage of natural gas into liquid petroleum enough to supply the world’s energy needs for the next 25 years. In addition to natural gas, large amounts of methane are available from coal beds and as byproducts of petroleum refining. The relative inertness of CH 4 has limited its application as chemical feedstock in spite of the relative abundance of this inexpensive hydrocarbon. It has been estimated that the methane byproduct being flared from crude oil fields is equivalent to about 1 million barrels of oil per day. Consequently, a long term research goal is the upgrading of methane into higher molecular weight hydrocarbons that are economically more valuable, more easily transportable or stored, and can be suitable feed stocks for current commercial petrochemical manufacturing processes. According to the assessment from Honeywell (UOP), the production of synthesis gas (syngas, consisting of a mixture of CO and H 2 ) is 80% of the cost of the indirect GTL process. Therefore, a more effective process which can avoid the production of syngas is explored. The direct route such as direct non-oxidative conversion of methane to aromatics (benzene and naphthalene) emerges. The most promising catalyst is the supported Mo/ZSM-5 catalyst for non-oxidative conversion of methane to aromatics. Supported molybdenum oxide catalysts are widely employed as commercial catalysts for hyrodesulfurization and hydrocracking of heavy fractions of crude oil, olefin metathesis, isomerization, hydrogenation and polymerization of alkenes in the petroleum industry, and partial oxidation of aliphatic alcohols 5 . The ZSM-5 is a type of aluminosilicate zeolite patented by Mobil which has a pore opening of about 5.5 Å in size similar to the size of a benzene molecule. It has been widely used in the petroleum industry as a heterogeneous catalyst for hydrocarbon isomerization reactions. The pioneering work of the activity of Mo/ZSM-5 catalysts in dehydro-aromatization of methane was reported by Wang 1 in 1993. Their supported Mo/ZSM-5 catalyst exhibited a high selectivity for methane towards benzene. Many researchers have reported the optimum catalytic activity of 7~ 12% CH 4 conversion and 70~100% selectivity towards benzene over Mo/ZSM-5 catalysts with 2~3 wt% molybdenum loading 1-4 . Supported Mo/ZSM-5 catalysts are able to convert methane to aromatics, but despite intensive studies there is no agreement in the catalysis literature about: the nature of supported Mo species on ZSM-5 (monomer, dimer or cluster) and anchoring site(s) of Mo species (Al-Al, Al-Si or Si-Si). The intense interest in supported molybdena catalysts has motivated numerous molecular structural characterization studies of the surface MoOx species: in situ Raman 6,7,8 , infrared (IR) 9, 10 , in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XANES/EXAFS) 14 , temperature programmed desorption (TPD)/temperature programmed reduction (TPR) 15 , X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) 16 , and UV-visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS) 16, 17 . These characterization investigations have significantly contributed to the fundamental understanding of supported molybdena catalysts and impacted both their fundamental research and industrial development efforts. In situ UV-vis DRS revealed that the initial supported MoO x are exclusively present as isolated monomeric surface sites on the ZSM-5 support. Combined in situ Raman spectroscopy and DFT calculations in H 2 18 O exchange, dehydrated Raman, and H 2 –TPR experiments, however, revealed the presence of four distinct surface MoO x structures on the Mo/ZSM-5 support: 1) isolated dioxo (O=) 2 MoO 2 surface site over two Brønsted acid sites at low Mo loading and high Al content at 998 cm -1 ; 2) isolated dioxo (O=) 2 MoO 2 surface site over one Brønsted acid site and an adjacent Si-OH group at increasing Mo loading at 970 cm -1 ; 3) isolated dioxo (O=) 2 MoO 2 surface site over two Si-OH groups at low Al content at 983 cm -1 ; 4) isolated mono-oxo O=MoO 4 surface site over extra framework Al-OH groups at high Al content found at 1026 cm -1 . In situ FT-IR showed that MoO x prefers to anchor at Brønsted acid sites at low Mo loading, and at Si-OH and external Al-OH groups at higher Mo loading and low Al content. The addition of MoO x to ZSM-5 also indicates dealumination and forms extra-framework Al 2 O 3 NPs. These new studies demonstrate how systematic studies with modern approaches to catalysis research are able to resolve the fundamental issues of complex catalytic systems and establish the relationships between the molecular and electronic structures of the catalytic active sites and the corresponding catalytic activity and selectivity performance. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Converged Free Energies of Binding in Cucurbit[7]Uril and Octa-Acid Host Systems from Expanded Ensemble Simulations
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Molecular containers, such as cucurbit[7]uril and the octa-acid cavitand host, have been used in a wide variety of applications, including selective drug delivery and release, specific molecular capture, and even for use in molecular machines such as nanoscale locks. Due to their ability to bind guests in a highly specific manner over a wide range of binding affinities, these small-molecule hosts are ideal test systems for optimizing and analyzing methods for computing free energies of binding that are also applicable to biologically relevant proteins. To this end, we have performed initially blind free energy calculations to determine the free energies of binding for ligands of both the cucurbit[7]uril and octa-acid hosts. A subset of the selected guest molecules were those included in the SAMPL4 prediction challenge, to which we made submissions for each host. For the expanded ensemble simulations that we have run, we are able to show that our estimates are converged and that the errors in our estimates are due only to the assigned force field parameters. This is confirmed through the use of alternative thermodynamic pathways, simulations of extended length, and analysis of sampled conformations. Our results also demonstrate the benefits of enhanced sampling of multiple local free energy minima imparted by the use of expanded ensemble molecular dynamics.

The spectral and directional optical properties are applied to a Monte Carlo ray-tracing model that determines the transport of the solar radiation within the cavity. The emitted radiative transfer is calculated using a Radiosity model, which is coupled to heat transfer, species transport, and chemical reaction kinetics in a computational fluid dynamics model. The absorbing cavity contains an array of reaction tubes, each with an inner porous medium of cobalt ferrites deposited on alumina substrates that undergo a two-step water splitting redox cycle to produce hydrogen. The simulation results examine material properties, geometries, operating conditions, cycle time, and solar profile shape, and the trends in aperture size, number of tubes, and amount of reaction material are further assessed. Performance is improved with a large number of small-diameter tubes; however, the tube placement within the cavity has minimal impact. Configurations for both isothermal and temperature swing operation are analyzed, and indicate that similar time-averaged solar-to-chemical efficiencies, accounting for O 2 separation and steam vaporization, of up to 14% are achievable.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: 1-Dimensional PCA Approach for Classifying Imbalanced Data Sets
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Varayini Pankayatselvan, Derrick K Rollins, Sr. “1-Dimensional PCA approach for classifying imbalanced data sets” Major: Chemical Engineering The goal of data mining is to uncover patterns within large sets of data as to reveal important information. It is a subfield of several disciplines, including statistics and computer science. Imbalanced binary data sets pose a challenge in extracting information to produce high classification results. Some methods developed to classify these sets involve multi-parametric classification algorithms such as SMOTE, neural network and random forest. These methods can produce relatively high classification results, however their methodology can also be very involved. In bypassing the complexity, we have developed two powerfully simple one-dimensional classification methods producing high summary statistics. We implemented and modified a one-dimensional, PCA based approach, previously developed by Rollins et al., to separate imbalanced data sets on seven cases. Based on this PCA separation, we have developed two new classification techniques: mean method and spread method. In addition, we have also developed a feature reduction method in which we found an increase in classification results. We observed improved or similar results when comparing our data from the seven case studies with a recently published study on LVQ-SMOTE done by Kanazawa University in Ishikawa Japan. The summary statistics were sensitivity, specificity, and g-mean. We note that only providing these statistics do not give enough information on the validity of the classification technique. We challenge that the actual values for true positives and false positives should be provided.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Insights into Dehydration of 1,2,6-Hexanetriol over Model Silica-Alumina Surfaces
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Increasing interests in the use of biorenewables feedstocks as alternatives to petroleum sources have promoted many of the recent studies in the literature on the dehydration, hydrogenolysis, decarbonylation and decarboxylation pathways of oxygenated intermediates derived from biomass. The selective dehydration and functionalization of polyols such as 1,2,6-hexanetriol to α,ω-diols are important paths that may enable the production of diacids, diamines, and lactones from renewable sources. Herein we use first-principle theoretical calculations to examine the reaction paths and mechanism involved in the dehydration of 1,2,6-hexanetriol over model silica alumina catalytic surfaces. More specifically, we carry out density function theory (DFT) calculations to examine the reaction pathways and elementary steps in the dehydration of 1,2,6-hexanetriol over a model 2D zeolite structures. Experimental results reported by Nolan and Shanks at ISU show significantly higher selectivities for the conversion of 1,2,6-hexanetriol to THP-2-M than to the more desired 6-hydroxyhexanal product. The results from theoretical calculations indicate that the intrinsic activation barriers for the formation of THP-2-M is 72 kJ/mol whereas the barrier to form 6-hydroxyhexanal is 84 kJ/mol (12 kJ/mol higher) which is consistent with the much higher selectivities to the THP-2-M product reported experimentally. The reaction of 1,2,6-hexanetriol to the THP-2-M proceeds via the protonation and elimination of the OH group at the 2-position of the triol to form a secondary carbenium ion that is stabilized by the direct interaction with the primary OH group at the 6-position to form a stable 6-member ring carbenium ion intermediate. The reaction of 1,2,6-hexanetriol to form the 6-hydroxyhexanal product also proceeds via the protonation and elimination of the OH group at the 2-position. The secondary carbenium ion that forms, however, is now stabilized by a hydride transfer from the 1- to the 2- position on the triol in order to localize the charge on the terminal OH group. DFT calculations were carried out on all of the other viable dehydration paths including the dehydration of the terminal OH groups at the 1- and 6-positions. The dehydration barriers at the primary 1- and 6- positions of 1,2,6-hexanetriol were all calculated to be at least 9 kJ/mol higher than those at the secondary position. The theoretical results also showed that 1,6 hexanediol can be formed via the dehydration of the primary OH groups along with an OH shift from the secondary carbon to the terminal carbon but requires significantly higher activation barriers. The main paths to THP-2-M and 6-hydroxyhexanal products were thus concluded to occur via the dehydration of the secondary OH intermediate. Theoretical results also indicate that the production of oxepan-3-ol is also possible via the dehydration of both of the terminal 1- and 6- OH species to form oxepan-3-ol with a barrier of 88 kJ/mol which is 16 kJ/mol higher than that to form THP-2-M. Finally, the ring opening of THP-2-M to hexanal was calculated to be 130 kJ/mol which indicates that THP-2-M is quite stable and does not react further which is consistent with the high selectivities measured experimentally. The mechanistic insights gleaned from this work help to advance our knowledge for the dehydration of polyols found in most biorenewables feeds and can be used to help to provide a more general understanding of the dehydrogenation reaction of polyols over acid catalysts.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Developing a System for Maintaining Ozone Levels in a Controlled Environment
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: A method for monitoring and maintaining ozone levels in a reaction chamber was developed. Process control methods and a base software system were developed and calibrated. A user-friendly interface was also created. Previously, it has been difficult to maintain constant ozone levels in the reaction chamber and most experimentalists have simply added an initial amount of ozone that was depleted with time. While convenient and considered a standard technique in the field, this method is not representative of the ambient atmospheric environment. We used a PID control system that would be able to maintain the ozone levels both efficiently and in a timely manner. The software to maintain the ozone levels was developed in LabVIEW, a program using a visual programming language. With this program, appropriate software was developed that would take in external data from an ozone meter, record and interpret it, and translate it into a usable signal that would be sent to an ozone generator, which would finally correct the ozone level in the reaction chamber. The hardware system assembled consisted of the previously mentioned ozone meter measuring the current ozone level in the reaction chamber, a computer which was situated in the lab and ran the designed program, a DC conversion box which interpreted the signal from the software and converted into a usable DC current, a AC conversion box which converted the DC current to a AC current, and the abovementioned ozone generator, which was powered from the AC conversion box. The calibration of the system involved determining the appropriate constants to use for the PID control system, which were originally determined using the Ziegler-Nichols tuning method and then heuristically altered to better control the ozone levels. The user-interface was further developed to include a computerized recording and transcribing of the ozone levels in the chamber, an ozone purge mode where the program would deactivate until the ozone levels reached zero, at which point it would start up again, and a bypass mode where the user could selectively add ozone without the PID controller correcting the ozone level. The control system developed introduces an exciting new opportunity for the study of atmospheric chemistry. In real world environments, ozone levels, on average, remain relatively constant within a given biome. However, in prior research, ozone was left to deplete to zero during the course of an experiment. Utilizing the new system, ozone levels can be maintained at any desired level, just as it would be in any real environment. This will allow for more accurate interpretations and understandings of the reactions that are studied in the laboratory.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Iron-Based Nanoparticles for the Removal of Arsenic, Lead, and Mercury Tegan Tingley, Liang Guo, Eric Wittgrove , and J.M. Calo Brown University, School of Engineering Providence, RI, 02912 Arsenic, lead, and mercury are well-known heavy metal toxicants. The primary goal of this research was to investigate the removal of these heavy metals from water using iron-based materials; namely, nanosize Fe 2 O 3 and Fe 3 O 4 (~100-200 nm), zero- valent iron (ZVI) chips (~1 mm), and nanosize colloidal rust (~20 nm) generated from the corrosion of 3 mm carbon steel spheres. Kinetic studies of arsenic removal demonstrated that the Fe 2 O 3 and Fe 3 O 4 removed arsenic best, both in terms of rate and ultimate equilibrium concentrations. Typically, arsenic was removed to less than the EPA MCL (10 µg/L) for drinking water (with a loading of 8 mg As/kg material). A single-pass system through a filter cake (collected on 0.1μm filter paper ), was also used in these investigations. Both synthesized arsenic solutions [ As( V) and As(III)] and well water samples from New Hampshire, containing high arsenic levels, were used in these studies. The influence of other parameters, such as pH, will also be discussed. The ZVI chips and Fe 3 O 4 were also found to be effective for the removal of both lead and mercury. These studies were conducted as part of a research program utilizing a novel hybrid spouted bed/filter system that both generates and utilizes colloidal rust to remove heavy metals from water.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Technical Design, Implementation and Optimization of an Atomic Layer Deposition Reactor and Its Control System
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Technical Design, Implementation and Optimization of an Atomic Layer Deposition Reactor and its Control System Michael Schaefer 1 , Mason Chilmonczyk 2 , Rudy Schlaf 3 1 Department of Physics, University of South Florida, Tampa 2 Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Florida, Tampa 3 Department of Electrical Engineering, University of South Florida, Tampa Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) is a thin film manufacturing process that allows for angstrom thick layers to be uniformly placed on surfaces (including complex geometries) using self termination reactions via unique precursor gasses (e.g. Trimethylaluminum, Water, Titaniumtetracloride, Ammonia, etc.). Other methods such as Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD) do not guarantee a precisely controlled uniform surface coating due to an inability of controlling the reactions taking place. Our design is advantageous because of the capability of studying manufactured films and interfaces directly via x-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS), ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy (UPS), and inverse photoemission spectroscopy (IPES). The combination of all three methods allows for a complete electronic structure analysis without taking the sample out of vacuum conditions, thus reducing the amount of surface contamination respectively surface oxidation under ambient conditions. This presentation covers the technical design and prototyping, control system, and implementation of the ALD reactor with an outlook on goals. The topics include: 1) Solidworks™ modeling and simulation, 2) Production and implementation of previously made designs, 3) Microcontroller usage (Arduino™, LabVIEW™) in an effort to control the necessary parameters like temperatures, pressures, injection timing, and carrier gas flow, 4) Printable circuit board (PCB) design (KiCAD™) and production based off of the prototyped setup, 5) Fabrication of a boxed control to ensure reliable use for an extended period of time, and 6) future optimization procedures and reaction control by studying the precursor injection behavior via differential pressure gauge readout.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: The Modeling and Optimization of the Catalytic Hydrogenation of Butyric Acid to Butanol
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Butanol production has become an increasingly important process because of its direct impact on fuel cost savings and furthermore the economy. Using algae as a feedstock for butanol production has proven to be an effective method and consists of two main steps: fermentation of algae to form butyric acid and conversion of butyric acid to butanol. A catalytic hydrotreater is currently being used for the second part of the process and is executed by adding hydrogen to the butyric acid to make butanol. In order to make butyric acid for this process, algal solution that was formed from the hydrolysis of algae is left to react in a fermentation broth and then filtered. Carbon dioxide and hydrogen are both removed from the fermentation broth in this process. This research focuses on the optimization of the hydrogenation process i.e. the optimal operating conditions to achieve high butanol yield using plug flow reactor kinetics. The main reactions occurring during the hydrogenation are (i) conversion of butyric to butyric acid to butanol (desired reaction) and (ii) the conversion of butanol to butane (undesired reaction). This study investigates this problem by using reaction kinetics, mathematical modeling in Matlab® and Excel as well as process simulation in Aspen. The data fit the model best when the reaction was first order in butyric acid and zero order in hydrogen. Arrhenius activation energies, frequency factors were obtained and used to calculate equilibrium constants which were then compared to the experimental values. The data suggests that highest butanol yield occurs at and shorter residence times and that the reaction rate for the desired reaction increases with increasing temperature.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Amylin, or Islet Amyloid Polypeptide (IAPP), a 37-residue polypeptide produced by beta cells, exists in vivo as an intrinsically disordered protein. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Textile Wastewater Treatment By Magnetic Nanoadsorbents
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The project: Nanotechnology for textile wastewater treatment Textile industries, which are major consumers of fresh water, release significant amount of colors or organic dyestuffs in their effluents. The presence of dyes in wastewater poses an environmental concern since these organic dyes are toxic to aquatic and non-aquatic life. Their toxicity is well documented. Therefore, removing dyes from wastewater is essential before discharging effluents into the environment. However, these dyes are difficult to remove, non-biodegradable and exist for a long time in the environment, which makes it challenging to the conventional wastewater treatment techniques. A number of chemical, physical and biological conventional treatment methods have been developed for decolourization of textile wastewater (dye effluents); including coagulation–flocculation, precipitation, oxidation, ion exchange and membrane filtration, adsorption onto activated carbon and low cost adsorbents, etc. These methods are found to be limited because of their high cost, ineffectiveness in meeting stringent effluent standards, and the huge amount of sludge they could generate. Currently, the application of nanotechnology (i.e., the technology related to the utilization of materials at nanoscale, 1-100 nm) has emerged as a fascinating area of interest for removal of various contaminants from wastewater effluents. Nanoparticles (NPs) are the drivers of the nanotechnology revolution. They display unexpected properties that differ from their bulk material counterparts. NPs pose high adsorption capacities and affinities because of their specific functionality and large specific surface areas, i.e., surface area per unit mass. Due to these unique properties, nanoparticles have potential applications for the treatment of textile wastewater. Another important advantage of using magnetic NPs for the removal of environmental pollutants lies on the fact that they cost-effectively meet the environmental regulation for wastewater treatment, as they can be prepared in situ where treatment is needed and recovered by simple magnet; translating into reduced operating and processing costs. In this project we aim at investigating the effectiveness of the magnetic iron oxide NPs in the removal of large organic contaminants (dyes) from real textile wastewater. This study provides valuable insight on the effect of NPs toward the treatment and recyclability of textile wastewater, which is crucial for the textile industry. In this study, a batch-contact-time method is used for the treatment of a real textile wastewater sample obtained from a local factory in the city of Nablus. The effects of different experimental parameters such as contact time, initial concentration, NPs dose, solution pH, and coexisting anions on dye removal are investigated. Results showed that dye adsorption was fast, and equilibrium was achieved within 10 min. The adsorption equilibrium data fit very well to Langmuir and Freundlich adsorption isotherm models. The thermodynamics studies indicated that the adsorption was spontaneous, endothermic and physical in nature. The desorption and regeneration studies have proven that NPs can be employed repeatedly without impacting its adsorption capacity. Therefore, magnetic NPs are recommended as fast, effective and inexpensive adsorbents for rapid removal and recovery of contaminants from wastewater effluents, like textile industry.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The Aerobic Cometabolic Transformation of Chlorinated Ethenes by the Mycobacterium ELW-1 Grown on Isobutene AUTHORS: Stephanie Rich 1 , Mohammad Azizian 1 , Michael Hyman 2 , Lewis Semprini 1 1 School of Chemical, Biological, and Environmental Engineering, Oregon State University; 2 Department of Microbiology, North Carolina State University. ELW1 is a recently isolated aerobic bacterium, in the mycobacterium family, that was discovered to have cometabolic capabilities, such as the ability to transform chlorinated ethenes into less toxic substances. The focus of this research was to determine the rates of transformation when this organism was exposed to high contaminant concentrations. This will help establish the practicality of using ELW1 for bioremediation techniques in the field. The chlorinated ethenes ELW1 was found to transform are notorious carcinogens, groundwater pollutants, and volatile organic compounds whose remediation has been a worldwide problem for over 40 years. Transformation rates for three different types of chlorinated ethenes were determined, (TCE), cis -dichloroethene (c-DCE), and vinyl chloride (VC). The ELW1 culture was grown and sustained in both batch culture and steady-state chemostat environments with isobutene as a growth substrate on a minimal growth media containing trace minerals, such as cobalt and a phosphate buffer. The batch-grown cells for these experiments were cultured in 600mL glass bottles with Teflon-lined septa, filled with 300mL of growth media. Batch cells were then harvested after a four-day incubation period at an optical density (OD 600 ) of approximately of 0.34, while chemostat -grown cells were harvested at an optical density (OD 600 ) of 1.3-1.5. Cells that were used for experiments were concentrated by centrifugation, washed with excess media and placed in a new media solution containing high concentrations of the compound to be tested. Initial rates of transformation were determined using gas chromatography to analyze 100µL samples of headspace gas over a period of one to three days to determine the rate of compound loss. The rates of utilization of a range of isobutene concentrations using batch-grown cultures were determined in order to estimate values of the half-substrate coefficient, K s and maximum utilization rate, k max . A K s value of 5.6 µ mol /L and k max value of 38 µ mol /day/mg protein was estimated for isobutene, which is in the range of values previously determined at North Carolina State University. Isobutene rate tests were performed using the same procedure as contaminant rate tests, over a range of isobutene concentrations. The rates at which ELW1 can utilize isobutene were compared with rates of chlorinated ethene transformation, which overall quantifies the practicality of using this organism in the field. The results of this type of comparison analysis are displayed in Table 1. Table 1 Transformation rates determined for ELW-1 grown on isobutene Cell Growth Compound Initial Liquid Concentration( umol /L) Rate of Transformation ( umol /day/mg TSS) Batch VC 421 5.1 Chemostat VC 382 3.2 Batch c -DCE 1330 4.1 Chemostat c -DCE 1400 3.5 Batch TCE 198 0.2 Batch Isobutene 118 15.9 Chemostat Isobutene 129 11.2 The values in Table 1 show that the ELW-1 culture can transform VC and c-DCE much faster than TCE. The rates measured using batch-grown cultures are consistently faster than the estimated rates obtained with the chemostat grown cells. By comparing the rate of TCE transformation with that of isobutene, it is not certain whether the ELW-1 culture would be effective for the bioremediation of TCE contamination. c -DCE and VC, however, would be effectively treated using ELW-1.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: The Effect of Stabilizers on the Ability of Zero Valent Iron Nanoparticles to Degrade Trichloroethylene
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Zero valent iron nanoparticles, particles with at least one dimension under 100 nanometers, have been found to be effective for remediation of groundwater contaminants due to their large surface area to volume ratio and high mobility in contaminated target zones. These properties cause the particles to rapidly agglomerate, which can decrease their reactivity. To overcome the attractive forces between the particles, a stabilizing compound can be added to the particle solution during synthesis. This study examined the stabilizing capabilities of gum arabic and sodium carboxymethyl cellulose and the effect of stabilization on particle reactivity. The ability of the stabilized particles to degrade trichloroethylene, a hazardous groundwater contaminant, over 24 hours was assessed using gas chromatography. The concentration of trichloroethylene incubated with unstabilized zero valent iron nanoparticles did not decrease at all, while the concentration of the trichloroethylene incubated with gum arabic stabilized particles decreased by about 12 percent. The small size and dispersion of the stabilized particles provided more reactive sites per particle than the unstabilized particles, leading to increased reduction of trichloroethylene.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Increased demand for and over-allocation of fresh water resources in the San Joaquin River Basin (SJRB) has necessitated the creation of real-time water quality management (RTWQM) strategies to ensure that downstream water quality objectives are met. The Grasslands Water District (GWD), 47,795 acres of natural and artificial seasonal wetlands, has been identified as an area of priority for real-time salinity management. Salinity in the GWD is of special concern as wetland drainage release periods correspond to periods of low assimilative capacity in the SJRB and the irrigation season of salt-sensitive crops. In this study, two proposed RTWQM models, Watershed Analysis Risk Management Framework (WARMF) and WetManSim, were evaluated using the concept of mass balance in order to validate their hydrological assumptions. Major mass imbalances were found in the WARMF model resulting in an average change in catchment storage capacity of ±2.02 feet per water year. This imbalance is most likely due to the lack of integration of irrigation demand calculations and artificial wetland flooding schedules. WetManSim was found to be in mass balance however the model is limited to average monthly as opposed to daily analysis. WARMF shows promise as a powerful water-quality management tool. Integration of an irrigation demand calculator could help more accurately represent inflows to land catchments. As WARMF and other RTWQM models advance it is important that users understand the assumptions behind each model and critically evaluate results before using them for environmental decision-making.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Seasonal Effects on the Ignition Characteristics of Live Fuels in Wildfires
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Wildfires are incredibly complex and costly to fight. Models are used to predict fire spread and plan control strategies, but are often inaccurate and computationally expensive. Additionally, much of the research that contributes to fire spread models focuses on dead and dried fuels, while fewer studies have been conducted on the combustion behavior of live, water-rich plants, which make up a significant portion of wildfire fuels. In order to improve fire spread models and understand the physical phenomena governing live fuel combustion, we are studying the effects of seasonal changes in moisture content and different heating modes (convective and radiative heat transfer) on the ignition, burning, and devolatilization characteristics of live samples of several species common to fire-prone areas of the United States. Experiments are conducted in a glass cage over a flat flame burner (FFB) fueled by a stoichiometric mixture of methane and hydrogen gas with a surface temperature of approximately 1000 °C; the apparatus also includes a radiant panel (25-32 W/in 2 ) adjacent to the cage that provides purely radiative heating to the sample. Over one year, a set of small samples (2-4 cm) of each participating species was burned each month, and raw data were collected via a video camera, IR camera, mass balance, and thermocouple to determine flame characteristics, surface temperatures, mass loss profiles, and gas temperatures, respectively. Data were collected and analyzed to determine the relationships between variables such as season, fuel moisture content, physical attributes, ignition time, ignition surface temperature, maximum flame height, flame duration, and mass loss rate. The first year of experiments, which comprised three species native to the western United States, showed that ignition and burning characteristics depended on season, moisture content, and heating mode, but that each species responded differently. Moisture content varied predictably with season, reaching a peak during the spring and decreasing through the summer and fall. Ignition time and surface temperature behaved similarly, but with more variance, suggesting that moisture content is not the only contributing variable. Mass loss profiles also varied significantly with season and moisture content. Averaged over the year, the data indicated that heating mode (convective heating only with the FFB versus convective heating combine with radiative heating from the radiant panel) had a significant effect for some of the variables. For instance, the addition of radiation clearly decreased ignition time and increased ignition surface temperatures. However, the effect on variables such as maximum flame height and mass loss rate was unclear. The second year of data collection, which comprises seven species native to the western and southern United States, is ongoing. Thus far, the data display the same trends in the effects of season and heating mode, but also reveal regional patterns. Species collected from the same geographical area show similar burning behaviors, even between different types of species. In addition, the second year data includes fuel density measurements that do not correlate well with other physical attributes, but also display regional patterns. The results thus far demonstrate that while both seasonal changes in moisture content and differences in heating mode affect burning behavior, neither factor accounts for all of the discrepancies in the data. Additionally, neither factor appears to represent major changes in the physical phenomena governing the burning characteristics of live fuels.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: The Effect of Ozone Stress on the Output of Volatile Organic Compounds and the Resulting Aerosol Properties Produced By Eastern White Pine
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The eastern white pine is a tree commonly found in North America. Several factors, such as temperature and light intensity, have been reported to be triggers of VOC emissions in plants. However, little is known about how plants react to abiotic stress, such as an impulse of increased ozone in the air around the plant. Previous studies have analyzed the particles that form when an eastern white pine branch is placed in an air environment with high amounts of ozone. This method had two shortcomings. First, the composition of the compounds given off by the stressed branch weren’t known. Second, additional stress was applied to the tree when cutting the branch sample, so the relative effects of the ozone stress were unknown. This study identified the compounds emitted from small eastern white pine trees under different levels of ozone stress using solid phase micro extraction (SPME) sampling method, which caused no damage or stress to the tree. The resulting aerosols produced at different ozone stress levels were analyzed using a scanning mobility particle sizer (SMPS) and cloud condensation nuclei counter (CCNC).

Titania nanotube, nanofiber, and nanoparticle electrodes were obtained through anodic oxidation of pure titanium sheet. Nanostructured Titania was further doped with palladium metal. It was found that titania nanotube electrode degraded the pollutant faster than palladium doped titania nanofiber and nanoparticle electrodes. Pd-doped titania nanotube electrode was the most effective in degrading methyl orange pollutant because of the very large surface area providing higher catalytic capability.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Kinetics and Rate Modeling of Chlorinated Aliphatic Hydrocarbon (CAH) Dehalogenation Using Anaerobic Cultures
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Kinetics and Rate Modeling of Chlorinated Aliphatic Hydrocarbon (CAH) Dehalogenation Using Anaerobic Cultures Jenny Green, Dr. Mohammad Azizian, Dr. Lewis Semprini Oregon State University; School of Chemical, Biological, and Environmental Engineering Corvallis, OR 97331 ABSTRACT Chlorinated aliphatic hydrocarbons (CAHs) were commonly used organic solvents. Their improper storage and disposal has resulted in widespread subsurface contamination. Bioremediation of CAHs is a promising solution to this problem and the in-situ option has been, and continues to be, investigated at Oregon State University. Some CAHs are under special scrutiny; perchloroethene (PCE), trichloroethene (TCE), cis -dichloroethene ( cis -DCE) and vinyl chloride (VC) in particular. PCE and TCE are common groundwater contaminants, and cis -DCE and VC are their anaerobic transformation products. By the process of dehalogenation , PCE can potentially be transformed to ethene , a non-toxic end product. The species of bacteria known as Dehalococcoides mccartyi is recognized for its ability to degrade PCE completely into ethene by means of halorespiration . These are the only known organisms with the ability to do so. Two cultures (EV and VS) containing strains of Dehalococcoides mccartyi are maintained under chemostat growth conditions in the bioremediation lab at Oregon State University and are the focus of this study. The objectives of this study were as follows: 1) To determine the rates that the culture in each chemostat can dehalogenate the CAH in question, and 2) To evaluate whether the initial CAH affected the transformation rates of the transformation products. The rate studies were conducted as batch kinetic tests with cells harvested from the chemostats . The methods described were used for each batch experiment with variation in the mass of CAH and hydrogen (H 2 ) gas additions. Batch experiments began by fitting three 125-mL glass reactors with screw-on caps and rubber septa in an anaerobic glove box (90:10 N 2 /H 2 ) and then removing them from the system. Using anaerobic methods, 50 mL of culture was added to each reactor and purged with anaerobic gas to eliminate residual CAHs and ethene . After purging, additions of CAH and H 2 were made depending on the experiment in question. The reactors were shaken for several minutes to equilibrate the liquid and gas concentrations. At fairly regular time intervals, 100 μL samples from the headspace of each reactor were analyzed using a HP-6890 GC to determine the CAH and ethene concentrations. The total masses of individual compounds in the reactor were calculated by mass balances using HenryÕs Law. Mathematical analysis and modeling of the experimental results was done using the methods described by Berggren (2011). The model determines the rate of transformation, K m X, for each step of the transformation process by simultaneously fitting the complete temporal data set. Minor adjustments were made to the modeling spreadsheets used for BerggrenÕs thesis to allow their use with other compounds. A process of Excel Solver utilization and value optimization provided an average K s and K corrected ­ value for each CAH tested and the best fit K m X value for each CAH that was transformed. In addition, linear fitting was also done to estimate K m X values. Rates for each compound were calculated by summing all of the rates of product formation at each instant of time. Linear regressions were run and the slopes were corrected using culture volume in order to compare with K m X values obtained from the modeling. Testing confirmed that, in general, cultures grown in 5-liter chemostats with excess electron donor added ( formate ) performed better in transforming VC to ethene than cultures fed limited donor in 2-liter chemostats . This is consistent with more complete transformation to ethene in the chemostats fed excess formate . In addition, the testing revealed that the culture harvested from the VS-5L chemostat performed better than the EV-5L chemostat culture. The VS-2L chemostat also performed better than the EV-2L chemostat . Overall, linear fitting rates were lower than modeling rates, since the linear method does not account for CAHs inhibiting the transformation of other CAHs, while the modeling-derived rates do. Although the modeling method functions well and fits the data well, it has a higher level of complexity and more variables are involved. A more in-depth analysis of the model-estimated rates is still needed. A focus of this study was to determine the affect that the initial CAH introduced to the reactors had on the rate of dehalogenation . The modeling method will confirm any observations when it is improved, but after a simple analysis, both linear and modeling patterns emerged suggesting that VC rates are similar regardless of initial CAH added. Another important observation is that both EV and VS have slower rates for all CAHs when beginning with PCE. An explanation for this is that all the chemostats were fed TCE, and therefore they may not be equipped with the enzymes that can rapidly dehalogenate PCE. The most variation in data occurs in the triplicates when PCE and TCE were added , where inhibition has the greatest affect on formation and degradation rates. Modeling methods will be improved so that the effects of initial CAH on dehalogenation rates can be solidified. Further testing and analysis are required to confirm all conclusions. REFERENCES Berggren, D. (2011). Kinetic and Molecular Effects of Sulfate Reduction on a Dechlorinating Culture under Chemostat Growth Conditions . Masters thesis. Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR.
