https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Plasmon Resonances in Bimetallic Nanostructures: The Role of Temperature and Core/Shell Architecture
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Bimetallic nanostructures are of significant technological interest due to their ability to synergistically combine properties of two distinct metals giving rise to multimodal characteristics. In this work, we have synthesized Au@Ag bimetallic nanostructures of three different geometries (nanocubes, nanopyramids, and nanorods) and investigated the role of thermal induction in controlling the nanostructure morphological evolution and the corresponding impact on the optical resonances. By increasing the reaction temperature from 28 °C to 150 °C we observe a red-shift in the plasmon resonance of the nanopyramids followed by a blue-shift at temperatures above boiling point of water; however, no appreciable shift was observed in the optical resonance of the nanocubes. The observed behavior was attributed to a combination of phase retardation effects, stability and critical micelle concentration of ligands, and energetics of the different crystal planes. We also investigated the formation dynamics and observed a sigmoidal growth at lower temperatures relative to an exponential growth at higher temperatures. The activation energy was calculated from the growth dynamics and the rate of nucleation was correlated to the reductive ability of ascorbic acid. Finally we also investigated the effect of core to shell ratio in determining the morphological evolution of bimetallic nanostructures.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Superhydrophobic Copper Foils Via Aqueous Ammonia Etching and Alkyltrichlorosilane Modification
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Using surface modification to generate unique properties on a variety of substrates has been a field of intense investigation in recent decades. One poster-child of this work has been the development of countless methods for achieving superhydrophobicity – that is, liquid contact angles in excess of 150° - on myriad substrates. However, this development has lagged for certain materials, such as engineering metals (copper, aluminum, etc.) and inorganic metal oxides, due to technical challenges associated with their high surface energies. In this work, a simple immersion method is presented as a route to superhydrophobicity on copper foils. The foil is cleaned ultrasonically and then etched in aqueous ammonia for 24-72 hours, allowing for evaporation of the etchant. Initially, oxygen adsorption corrosion drives the dissolution of copper. After some time, a copper hydroxide precipitate forms and slowly deposits as a patina layer on the copper surface. When evaporation is complete, the copper hydroxide coated foil is exposed to an alkyltrichlorosilane, and subsequently, water contact angles as high as 165º may be observed.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Linear-Low Polyethylene Nanocomposite Fabrication Via Solid-State/ Melt Extrusion
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Linear-Low Polyethylene Nanocomposite Fabrication via Solid-State/ Melt Extrusion David A. Frey and Katsuyuki Wakabayashi Department of Chemical Engineering Bucknell University Lewisburg, PA 17837 Combining a commercial polymer with an advanced filler material can yield a composite with a range of enhanced properties. Nanocomposites have recently been of interest because the nano -scale of the filler can impart unique properties for very low loading percentage. The production of these nanocomposites has been accomplished through several methods, but the knowledge about their differences is limited. The most common method in industry is twin-screw extrusion (TSE). This method uses a heated extruder barrel to disperse the filler in a molten polymer matrix. In contrast to this method, solid-state shear pulverization (SSSP) uses a chilled barrel to produce nanocomposites . Shear and compressive forces pulverize and mix the two materials, yielding a powder product. A recently developed process, solid-state/ melt extrusion (SSME), attempts to combine the benefits of both previous processes and uses a barrel split between cold and hot sections. Due to the differences in nature of these processes, variations in the properties and performance of the resulting nanocomposite products are expected. TSE is able to hold high production output while SSSP attempts to produce the most consistent and physically enhanced product throughout its powder producing processing. SSME allows for an increase in production rate similar to TSE and emulates the pulverization section of the SSSP process. This study compares the TSE, SSSP, and SSME processing on several model linear low-density polyethylene-based nanocomposites. Various types of carbon-based fillers, namely graphite, carbon nanotubes, and carbon black, were employed as fillers to observe differences in the physical properties of the outputs. Mechanical properties were determined via tensile-testing, while degradation behavior was examined via thermogravimetric analysis. Interpreting these results leads to predictions about how different processing affects the morphology of nanocomposites.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Strong Glycosaminoglycan Hydrogels for Tissue Engineering Applications
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Hydrogels are hydrophilic materials that typically contain over 95% water and are widely used in tissue engineering and drug delivery applications. However, due to high water content, hydrogels are weak and brittle. Therefore, methods to improve their mechanical performance (especially moduli and fracture strain) are highly sought. For tissue engineering scaffolding purposes, glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), such as hyaluronic acid (HA) and chondroitin sulfate (CS) have been of great interest for hydrogels since they are biocompatible and abundant in the mammalian extracellular matrix. However, like many other hydrogels, GAG based hydrogels typically do not possess the mechanical properties that are needed for a mechanically robust tissue engineering scaffold. To address this problem, in this study functionalized (methacrylated) HA and CS were photo-copolymerized with acrylate oligomers of ethylene glycol. The hypothesis was that acrylate oligomers of ethylene glycol could improve the crosslink density of the copolymer gels by improving the reaction yield through bridging the macromere functional groups with the crosslinker and grow the kinetic chains, which otherwise due to steric limitations would not be possible. Methacrylated hyaluronic acid (MHA) was co-polymerized with acrylate ethylene glycol (EG) oligomers with lengths varying from (EG) 2 DA to (EG) 13 DA . It was found that as the lengths of the EG oligomers increased, the shear modulus, Young’s modulus, and crosslink density of the co-polymerized gels improved. When the crosslinker spacer length increased from (EG) 2 DA to (EG) 13 DA, the shear modulus increased from 191 kPa to 268 kPa while the Young’s modulus increased from 658 kPa to 949 kPa. The crosslink density was increased from 0.824 mol/cm 3 to 0.962 mol/cm 3 for (EG) 2 DA and (EG) 13 DA respectively. As buffer solutions are used in tissue engineering practices, the salt effect on swelling, moduli, and the crosslink density of these gels were studied. For this purpose, methacrylated chondroitin sulfate (MCS) was equilibrated in salt solutions of different ionic strengths (0.01M to 1.4M sodium chloride solutions). For a MCS 13 wt% gel, it was found that as the salt concentration increased, the swelling degree decreased from 42 to 8. Additionally, for the same range of salt concentration the shear modulus decreased from 47 kPa to 9 kPa and the Young’s modulus decreased from 141 kPa to 27 kPa. With increasing salt concentration, the crosslink density decreased from 0.256 mol/cm 3 to 0.0277 mol/cm 3 .

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Effects of Non – Thermal, Atmospheric, Argon – Based Plasma on the Surface Properties of Human Dentin for Adhesive Applications
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The dental industry has long been hindered by poor adhesion quality between the dentin and enamel with dental composite during restoration. The result of this is restorations being performed on teeth that have previously been restored, which causes a significant loss of tooth mass. A study of the effects of plasma treatment on the tooth-adhesive interface was conducted. Tensile strength tests on treated and untreated specimen indicate that plasma treatment has a noticeable effect on the strength of the adhesive. Wetting ability of the adhesive, tested qualitatively with contact angle data, indicates that plasma treatment plays a significant role in tooth surface energy and adhesive wetting ability. These results indicate that plasma treatment can potentially result in a stronger, longer lasting adhesive with less tooth loss.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Synthesis and Characterization of Curcumin Dimethacrylate to Synthesize Biodegradable Poly(B-Amino Ester) Antioxidant Polymers
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Curcumin is a well-known antioxidant which has been shown to relieve oxidative stress and assist in the wound healing process. However, previous attempts to deliver curcumin as an antioxidant drug have met with limited success, due to the low bioavailability of curcmin and the rapid degradation of curcumin in the body. Therefore, it is desirable to convert curcumin to biodegradable poly(β-amino ester) (PBAE) polymers which would protect curcumin from this rapid degradation, and which could be applied directly to the wound site. The polymer would release curcumin as the polymer degrades, aiding in the wound healing process. We have previously synthesized PBAE polymers using curcumin diacrylate (CDA). However, given the high reactivity of acrylate groups to primary amines (Michael Addition reaction), polymerization was difficult to control, resulting in polymers with suboptimal physical characteristics and degradation properties. As the methacrylate functional group is typically less reactive than the acrylate analog, it is hypothesized that the polymerization rate can be better controlled by the use of curcumin dimethacrylate (CDMA) versus a diacrylate system. In this work, CDA and CDMA monomers were synthesized and subsequent polymers are compared qualitatively, visually, and via polymer degradation. We found that CDMA is much less reactive than CDA; so much so, that the CDMA-based PBAE hydrogels degrade much too rapidly, probably because of significantly lower crosslinking.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Examining Cytoskeletal Organization and Cell Morphology on P(MEO2MA-co-OEGMA) Thermoresponsive Biomaterials of Variable Lower Critical Solution Temperature
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Thermoresponsive polymer (TRP) substrates as in vitro cell culture platforms have recently gained popularity due to their ability to release cells from the growth substrate without biochemical enzymes and while maintaining cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. Cells grown on TRPs are released from their culture surface by a simple change in temperature below the lower critical solution temperature (LCST) of the polymer. P(MEO2MA-co-OEGMA) substrates offer a unique advantage over PNIPAM, the gold standard: the ability to tune the LCST. In this work, we investigate cell growth on four P(MEO 2 MA-co-OEGMA) substrates of varying LCST using immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy. The effects of tunable LCST on cell adhesion was also investigated using contact angle as a proxy for cellular adhesion. Specifically, we quantified the equilibrium spreading coefficient of P(MEO 2 MA-co-OEGMA) thermobrushes with aqueous LCSTs of 28, 31, 34, and 37°C as a function of temperature and examined cell height and cytoskeletal organization over the course of 48 hours. Results show that surface hydrophobicity increases as LCST decreases, with LCST of 28 o C being the most hydrophobic surface. Phase contrast microscopy images revealed an increase in cell adhesion as a function of LCST, with the most hydrophobic surface (28 o C) promoting cell spreading comparable to a TCP control. Cell height also varied with changing LCST. In conclusion, thermoresponsive brushes synthesized from random copolymers of 2-(2-methoxyethoxy)ethyl methacrylate (MEO 2 MA) and oligo(ethylene glycol) methacrylate (OEGMA) (P(MEO 2 MA-co-OEGMA)) that exhibit variable aqueous LCST values can be used to promote cell adhesion in tissue engineering applications.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Analysis of Graphene-like Structures Produced from Commercial Graphite Via Solid-State Shear Pulverization
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Analysis of graphene-like structures produced from commercial graphite via solid-state shear pulverization Paola Arias and Katsuyuki Wakabayashi Department of Chemical Engineering Bucknell University Lewisburg, PA 17837 2013 Nanocomposties are advanced materials that incorporate nanosized particles into a polymer matrix. These nanocomposites possess enhanced properties of strength, light weight, durability and heat resistance. One of the materials of considerable interest to use as filler is Graphene. Graphene is a carbon structure, 2-dimensional crystal, the thinnest, lightest, strongest material. Due to its outstanding properties at a molecular scale there has been a great deal of effort in obtaining this material using complex experiments. In the polymer processing laboratory at Bucknell, we possess a unique machine called the solid-state shear pulverization (SSSP) and solid state melt extrusion (SSME). This machine pulverizes the polymer and filler together, causing the graphite particles to separate from each other via a process called exfoliation, which separates the individual graphene layers and increases the surface area.[1] This study focuses on the fabrication of new, superior, graphene-like structures from three different types of commercially available graphite using solid state shear pulverization (SSSP) and solid state melt extrusion (SSME). In addition, structures fabricated from carbon nanotubes and carbon black were fabricated and compared to the structures obtained from graphite. The analysis was primarily conducted through BET surface area measurement techniques and Scanning Electron Microscope to compare the exfoliated filler properties. Sonication was also used to determine if exfoliation of the samples processed through the SSSP and SSME methods are affected by the additional process. [1] K. Wakabayashi, P.J. Brunner, J. Masuda, S.A. Hewlett, J.M. Torkelson. Polymer, Volume 51, Issue 23, 29 October 2010.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Combustion Synthesis and Optical Property Tuning of Cerium Activated Gadolinium Aluminum Garnet (GAG) Phosphor Powders
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Cerium-doped gadolinium aluminum garnet (GAG:Ce) can be used to improve the efficiency of white-light LEDs (light emitting diodes). The Rogers group has gained expertise in combustion synthesis of yttrium aluminum garnet doped with Ce and/or Eu, however the process procedure does not produce good quality, pure phase GAG. This project focused on developing a gel-combustion synthesis of GAG:Ce. Photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy, powder x-ray diffraction (XRD), and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were used to characterize the effects of processing conditions on the resulting materials’ properties. Fuel type, combustion temperature, annealing temperature and annealing time were investigated. XRD showed that nearly pure phase GAG was formed by using citric acid as the fuel, a combustion temperature of 500°C, and a 4.5 hour, 1100 °C anneal. The trends observed in our results are consistent with phase diagrams that indicate pure-phase GAG should be formed at 1200 °C and above. Material combusted at 400 °C and annealed for 14 hours at 1100 °C had the most intense PL emission but did not contain the most garnet phase of the materials produced. This observation indicates PL emission intensity depends on factors in addition to crystal phase. We investigated the effects of substituting host ions on GAG PL intensity. Yttrium was substituted for gadolinium, and gallium was substituted for aluminum in the GAG lattice. XRD and XPS analyses were used to interpret the trends in PL emission of these host-doped materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Cavitation Rheology
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Cavitation rheology is the study of the mechanical behavior of gels and other soft solids upon the introduction of cavities. In this project we applied cavitation rheology to measure the elastic modulus of a triblock copolymer gel. Gels were obtained by dissolving 5% and 10% volumes of a triblock copolymer, poly(methyl methacrylate)–poly(n-butyl acrylate)–poly(methyl methacrylate), in 2 ethyl-1-hexanol. In these experiments a needle connected to a syringe was inserted in the gel. The air within the syringe was compressed at different rates, ranging from 0.1 to 5 mL/min, using an automated syringe pump, causing a buildup of pressure and leading to cavitation in the form of a rapidly growing bubble. The pressure at which the gel cavitates is called the critical pressure, and is related to the Young’s modulus, or elasticity, of the gel plus the surface tension between the gel and the air and the inverse of the size of the needle tip, which was varied by using needles of different diameters. Both the critical pressure and the size and nature of the bubble are being analyzed to investigate the mechanical behavior of these gel at any arbitrary locations within the material.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Behavior of Particles As Tunable Emulsion Stabilizers
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Behavior of Particles as Tunable Emulsion Stabilizers Institute: City College of New York Topic: Fuels, Petrochemicals, and Energy Student's Name: Jannatul Ferdaous Mentor's Name: Ilona Kretzschmar PhD Candidate's Name: Sepideh Razavi Abstract Emulsions exist in our daily lives as natural and manufactured systems. Emulsion stability or instability is a huge concern for the industrial branched of pharmaceuticals, personal care, and oil recovery. It is expected for every pharmaceutical and food emulsion to aspire utmost stability which will help maintain the product's quality and conduct over a certain period of time. Adjusting the stability of emulsions can contribute immensely in development of new materials, regulating chemical reactions and new separation mechanism. Our primary goal of this research is to investigate the effect of modified particles on emulsion stability, and how their role differentiates from that of a simple surfactant in an emulsion. One of our main objectives of this research is to prove our hypothesis that unmodified and modified particles are capable of increasing the stability of emulsions. This past summer, a PhD candidate, Sepideh Razavi, and I worked on understanding the characteristics of oil-in-water emulsions. We used hexadecane and dilute aqueous KNO3 solution (10-4 M) to make emulsions, which we then centrifuged to increase the speed of coalescence and separation of oil and water phases. The longer time and the stronger centrifugal force a sample of emulsion requires to separate, the more stable the emulsion is. We tried to produce the most stable emulsions possible without the addition of particles by varying one of the many parameters in each experiment. After a number of experimental trials, we have settled on a 1:1 of oil and water mixture and an emulsification time of 60s to produce the most stable emulsion possible without particles. Eventually we progressed to experimenting with unmodified silica (SiO2) particles. We have worked with three different sizes (250nm, 500nm, and 1um) of particles to compare the effect they have on emulsion stability. As we proposed in our hypothesis, the particles did enforce a greater stability on the emulsion which enabled us to separate the process of coalescence from creaming. This leads us to the conclusion that particles can be used to produce stable emulsion, which can be very beneficial for pharmaceuticals and personal care industries.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Development of Electrically Controlled Elastofluidic Robots and Microfluidic Devices
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Development of Electrically Controlled Elastofluidic Robots and Microfluidic Devices Kevin Nagle Advisor: Brandon Vogel Department of Chemical Engineering Soft shelled robotics is a new growing field. Requiring less power and able to work at lower pressures, soft robotics could replace hard bodied robotics in many applications of chemical, mechanical and even biomedical engineering. These soft shelled devices are made using an elastomer gel with reinforced fibers. Two layers of gel of sealed together to create small air tight chambers. By pumping a fluid, such as air, into these chambers at low pressures, one would cause the chambers to expand. The fibers control the ways in which the devices bend when the fluid is pumped into the chambers. If one controls how these chambers expand and contract one could cause one of these robots to move around or even walk. The combination between the elastic membranes and hydraulics is known as elastofluidics. These soft shelled elastofluidic devices are known as fiber reinforced elastomers or FRE for short. The research goal is to cause this expansion of the gel to be caused be an electrical stimulation rather than the introduction of a fluid through a pump. This would allow for greater applications of these devices and make the mechanisms that work these devices to be much smaller. Research has shown that electrical stimulations can cause gels to expand and contract, by putting a controlled voltage through the device we hope to stimulate what occurred by pumping a fluid into one of the devices. The goal was to inject the gel with the ionic liquid into the silicone casing to create the device. The electrical stimulation would be conducted by the ionic liquid in order to stimulate the gel. In addition to working on the elastofluidic devices I also did work with microfluidic devices. Microfluidic devices were sent to the Geisinger Medical Center of Pennsylvania for use in cancer research. The devices are used by passing drugs or fluids through the channels. The devices were created using PDMS. SU-8 was used to create a master silicon wafer in order to leave the print in the PDMS.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Investigating the Properties of ZnO:Al Buffer Layers, Deposited By ALD, for Thin-Film CIGS Solar Cells
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: CIGS is a tetrahedrally-bonded semiconductor material that can be used in thin film photovoltaic cells. Particularly, it is a very promising and growing absorber technology for the p-type absorber layer of CIGS solar cells. On the other hand, the standard material used for the n-type buffer layer in CIGS solar cells is Cadmium sulfide (CdS). However, CdS is toxic and absorbs unwanted blue light and UV light. We would like to find a good alternative buffer layer as a possible replacement for CdS. Such buffer layers can be effectively deposited by thin film deposition technique called ALD. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is capable of depositing a variety of materials by gas-surface reaction methods. The motivation to use ALD to deposit n-type buffer layers is due the conformality of ALD-deposited films on rough films, as well as the uniformity in the resulting alloy composition both laterally and with regards to thickness. One buffer layer material that we have deposited via ALD on CIGS is Zinc Oxide (ZnO). Zno is used in channels called point contacts, which have been found to increase CIGS solar cell performance. To reduce the influence of interference recombination, one can passivate the p-n junction surface, except in a few places where one can create conductive channels with a transparent conductor (i.e. ZnO). Typically the conductivity of a buffer layer made of ZnO can be increased by 10-100 times when doped with Al. In our lab, we have been varying this Al:ZnO ratio, as well as the temperature of the ALD chamber to achieve lower resistivity values.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: A Method for Clean H2 Generation from Solar Heat and Water
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Solar thermal water splitting is a method to transform diffuse, temporal, solar energy into a useful chemical fuel, namely H 2 that can be stored, transported and efficiently used. Solar thermal water splitting occurs when a metal oxide, “hercynite” material in this study, is heated using solar thermal energy to above 1200 o C where by it reduces generating oxygen. Traditionally, the material is then cooled ~ 300-500 o C below the thermal reduction temperature and exposed to steam whereby the steam re-oxidizes the metal oxide and produces H 2 gas. The metal oxide is subsequently cycled between the oxidation and reduction steps resulting in an overall reaction of H 2 O + solar thermal energy → H 2 + ½O 2 . The “hercynite” material used experimentally was synthesized using atomic layer deposition (ALD). ALD is a thin film coating technique that allows for a layer-by-layer deposition of metal oxides at the desired ratios and thickness. Thin films with high porosity are desired as they allow for decreased diffusional and thermal resistances. We demonstrate water splitting cycles using “hercynite” active material where the oxidation and reduction steps are carried out under isothermal conditions and that this is beneficial from an efficiency, total hydrogen generation, and material thermal stress standpoint. Additionally, in collaboration with Sandia National Laboratories, a follow up investigation of isothermal solar thermochemical cycling was carried out in order to better understand the cycle capacity and hydrogen productivity of hercynite materials over a range of operating temperatures and reactive gas partial pressures.

When delithiation occurs, a void space will be left that perfectly accommodates the large volumetric changes of silicon the next lithiation step. We successfully fabricated several porous carbon thin films with and without lithium silicide. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Thermal Properties and Ultrafast Dynamics of Phase Change Materials
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Phase Change Materials (PCMs) are materials which can be repeatedly switched between two or more phases; one amorphous and one or more crystalline. With a growing interest in the applications of PCMs, especially for improved solid-state memory technology, it is becoming more important to gain a fundamental understanding of the dynamics of their switching in order to design materials with faster switching speeds. Our emphasis was on the kinetics of PCM samples as they are heated and the impact this heating has on their transmission. The two methods used to measure the temperature dependence were a pump-probe test and FTIR spectroscopy. The most significant result, found in both the pump-probe tests and the FTIR, was that transmission of the materials decreased as temperature increased. Long-term effects from heating were also witnessed. One millisecond after being struck by the pump beam and one hour after being heated to 65° C in the FTIR, the transmission had not yet returned to its original value. The future of this project focuses on altering the pump-probe measurement to ensure the witnessed effects are caused by thermal, not electrical, changes of the PCM. This will be accomplished by measuring the temperature jump induced by the pump and comparing it to the FTIR measurements and by decreasing the rep-rate of the pump to find a change in the long-term effects on transmission. With a better understanding of the kinetics of change in these materials, and the electric field-driven switching dynamics, we will be able to store our data reliably and compactly; vital characteristics of data storage in an increasingly mobile world.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Metamaterials have the potential to yield flat lenses, diffraction-unlimited microscopes, and even invisibility cloaks. A metamaterial’s optical properties are governed by the spacing and alignment of small nanostructures embedded inside the material. These nanostructures, through electrical and magnetic coupling, may give rise to a negative index of refraction over a specific electromagnetic frequency – a phenomenon not found anywhere in nature. However, fabrication of theorized Negative Index Metamaterials (NIMs), and other novel structures, has been difficult due to the limitations of 3D nanofabrication. This study proposes a new technique that utilizes Nano-Sphere Lithography (NSL) and spin-coating to stack metasurfaces and create 3D metamaterials. We demonstrate the stacking of up to 3 NSL-defined metasurfaces, with no indication of a physical limit to how many layers can be stacked. The technique, hence, makes it more feasible to fabricate novel 3D metamaterials while still maintaining the resolution and simple fabrication offered by NSL.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Organic Monolayers on p-Doped Silicon Affect Photocurrents of Photosystem I Films
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Biohybrid solar cells convert light energy to electricity through the use of Photosystem I (PSI), a protein complex that drives photosynthesis in green plants. The near-one-hundred percent quantum efficiency of PSI, in addition to its vast abundance in nature, gives this technology enormous potential as a sustainable source of energy. Prior work from our group has shown that PSI films on p-doped silicon yield photocurrents that approach 1 mA/cm 2 , far exceeding those for unmodified silicon or for PSI on metals. In this project, we have investigated the use of organic monolayers deposited between the p-doped silicon semiconductor and the PSI layer to facilitate electron transfer and increase the stability of the PSI film. These monolayers were prepared by exposing silicon to solutions containing ω-terminated alkynes to produce an alkenyl attachment of the monolayer to silicon and create a surface of the ω-terminated functionality for interaction with PSI. Of the monolayer surface groups tested, including alcohols, amines, and carboxylic acids, the carboxylic acid terminus most consistently achieved the highest photocurrents, suggesting favorable electrostatic attraction between the negative surface of the monolayer and positive patches on PSI. Carboxylic acids of varying carbon chain lengths—specifically three, six, and seven carbons—were then tested using photochronoamperometry in order to observe the effect of monolayer thickness on photocurrent as well as the stability of the photocurrent over time. Differences in monolayer thickness did not have a noticeable impact on current, but all carboxylic acid-treated silicon samples retained over 60 percent more of their initial photocurrent density than the plain silicon control after 30 minutes of continuous testing.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Development of Antibody-Conjugated Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles for Biomedical Applications
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Background: There is significant interest in antibody-conjugated Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles (MSNPs) due to their potential uses as drug/siRNA carriers, as well as imaging agents with enhanced detection limits. Current imaging techniques like immunofluorescence (IF) and flow cytometry methods require the use of a primary antibody and fluorescent secondary antibody and are known for having problems with photobleaching and imaging sensitivity. We believe that antibody-conjugated MSNPs are a promising alternative to both the primary and secondary antibody. For one, fluorescent MSNPs have been found to be more photostable than the fluorescent dye itself, and therefore less susceptible to photobleaching. These antibody-conjugated MSNPs may also aid in signal amplification, increasing their sensitivity for use in detecting low-abundance proteins in cells. Finally, antibody-conjugated MSNPs contain a variety of other valuable features including relative ease of synthesis, batch-to-batch reproducibility, modifiability, a large surface area relative to its size, and pores for drug/probe loading. Methods/Characterization: Our current synthesis procedure was divided into three distinct steps: 1) Micelle Template Formation, 2) Silica Condensation, and 3) Template Removal (by acidic reflux). After MSNP synthesis, DLS was used to measure the hydrodynamic size and charge of the MSNPs. Then, to functionalize the nanoparticles, the MSNPs were coated first with Polyethyleneimine (PEI) and then with Polyethylenegylcol (PEG) before conjugating an antibody targeting a given protein. We found that it was possible to modify the surface groups of the nanoparticles by introducing different silanes 15 minutes after TEOS co-condensation. These modifications included: using (3-Mercaptopropyl) trimethoxysilane to for thiol surface groups and (3-Aminopropyl) trimethoxysilane for amine surface groups. We tested for the presence of these groups using Ellman’s Reagent and Fluorescamine assays. This surface modification was utilized for direct conjugation of antibody to nanoparticles, having PEG as a spacer. BCA/microBCA assays were also used to characterize the loading amount of antibody on the nanoparticles. We conjugated our developed MSNP with Trastuzumab (Herceptin) -- an antibody targeting the Human Epidermal Growth Factor 2 (HER-2) protein. This nanoconstruct was in turn evaluated for application in breast cancer targeting and treatment in our lab. Results: On average, we found that the size of nanoparticles synthesized this way were 70nm in diameter. The MSNPs were also found to have a negative charge of approximately -23mV in water. Additionally, due to our low Polydispersity Index (PDI) values (~0.002), and monodispersed size distribution, our nanoparticles hold great potential for development as antibody probes or drug carriers. The application of these developed mesoporous silica nanoparticles is currently under extensive investigation in our lab.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Surface Properties of Lithium Sulfide from First Principles
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Research interest in Lithium/Sulfur batteries has risen dramatically most recently due to the system’s potential to replace lithium-ion technology in selected applications. The Li/S system seems promising due to its high theoretical specific capacity (1166 mAh/g) and cheap, readily-available constituent materials. Implementation, however, has been plagued by problems in achieving suitable reversibility. These problems are due primarily to a lack of bulk electrical conductivity in the battery couple’s discharge product, Li 2 S, which disallows a reverse electrochemical reaction. It is possible, however, that this material has one or more stable surfaces which do conduct. In this work, we use ab-initio methods to study the thermodynamic stability of varying surfaces of Li 2 S, and whether these surfaces manifest conducting properties. We also study the adsorption trends of Li and S onto the most stable surface in order to better understand the growth mechanism of Li 2 S films.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Nanoparticle-Decorated Honeycomb-Structured Polymeric Films Via Breath Figures with Janus Particles
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The breath figures (BFs) patterning technique represents a simple, robust method for producing microstructured honeycomb-patterned porous polymer films. Amphiphilic “Janus” nanoparticles were expected to optimize the films with regards to nanoparticle enrichment in the pore walls as well as ordering degree of the honeycomb structures given their dual role as Pickering emulsion stabilizing agents and as highly effective solid surfactants, providing a significant improvement over what has been achieved using isotropic nanoparticles. A reliable method for producing optimal colloidosome coverage was established. Characterization of the films’ morphologies will help draw conclusions on the interfacial behavior and self-assembly performance of the Janus particles, as well as the general mechanism of BFs structure formation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Crystal Structure and Morphology of Adipic Acid/PVP Particles Formed via Monodisperse Droplet Evaporation Tara L. Panzarino Advisor: Ryan C. Snyder Bucknell University, Department of Chemical Engineering Particle characteristics and formation play a large role in the pharmaceutical industry. The characteristics of the particle determine the effectiveness and quality of the final drug product. In particular, the degree of crystallinity of the active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) can impact the dissolution and bioavailability of the API. Amorphous particles are desirable because they have higher solubility than any of the crystalline forms; however they are not always easy to produce. The goal of this work is to obtain amorphous particles of adipic acid, with the addition of an excipient. The resulting particles are compared to the morphology and crystallinity of particles formed only with adipic acid. In this work, the primary excipient considered is Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP). Particles of adipic acid and PVP are formed from the evaporation of monodisperse droplets produced from a Vibrating Orifice Aerosol Generator (VOAG). The VOAG creates monodispersed particles by applying a constant frequency across a solution jet to create droplets. These droplets are then allowed to dry in a column, and the particles can be collected and analyzed. Solutions of varying weight % ratios of adipic acid and PVP in isopropanol were considered. Particles of Adipic Acid and PVP were analyzed for structure using X-ray Diffraction. The results show that as the ratio of Adipic Acid to PVP became smaller, the particles became less crystalline in nature, with a transition around 50 weight % of each component. Morphology is also analyzed with SEM imaging. The morphology changes such that as the weight % ratio of Adipic Acid decreased, the particles became increasingly smooth. Adipic Acid particles ran through the VOAG in solutions of isopropanol typically have a wrinkled appearance, with a hole somewhere on the particle. Future plans also are presented.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Crystallization Kinetics of Polylactic Acid (PLA) Processed through Solid-State/Melt Extrusion
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Polylactic acid (PLA) is a bio-based polymer derived from corn, sugar beets, and other natural sources. It has recently become of interest because of its biodegradability and similarity in properties to other petroleum-based polymers. However, the widespread use of PLA is currently hindered by its inherently slow crystallization kinetics relative to other commercial polymers. The desired semi-crystalline structure is difficult to achieve in a reasonable amount of time when extrusion and other melt-molding techniques are used. Many different methods have been attempted in enhancing the crystallization kinetics of PLA. One of the most prominent is nucleating agents. While effective, this method is not environmentally friendly and can be very costly. An alternative is processing via solid-state shear pulverization (SSSP), a method developed by Northwestern University. SSSP has been shown to lead to faster crystallization kinetics in both PLA and polyethylene terephthalate (PETE) without any additives or blend components. We have recently developed a related extrusion technique called solid-state/melt extrusion (SSME). SSME combines traditional twin-screw extrusion (TSE) and SSSP. SSME is designed to combine the advantages of these two processes in an attempt to increase the rate of crystallization for faster, more productive processing. So far, SSME has been shown to be an effective processing method for polypropylene and polyethylene blends. This study explores the crystallization behavior and physical properties of PLA processed via SSME. The effectiveness of processing was assessed by comparing the properties of SSME-processed samples to those of TSE and SSSP. The rate and level of crystallization was measured by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), while degradation behavior and mechanical properties were analyzed via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and tensile testing, respectively.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: The Effect of Free Radical Inhibitor on the Sensitized Radiation Crosslinking and Thermal Processing Stabilization of Polyurethane Shape Memory Polymers
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The effects of free radical inhibitor on the electron beam crosslinking and thermal processing stabilization of novel radiation crosslinkable polyurethane shape memory polymers (SMPs) blended with acrylic radiation sensitizers have been determined. The polyurethane SMPs in this study possess novel processing capabilities. These SMP’s have the ability to be melted and processed into complex geometries as thermoplastics and then crosslinked using electron beam irradiation in a final curing step. This novel method is potentially much more cost effective and efficient than current methods when high throughput is desired. To increase the effectiveness of radiation crosslinking, the radiation sensitizer pentaerythritol triacrylate (PETA) was solution blended with thermoplastic polyurethane SMPs synthesized from 2-butene-1,4-diol and trimethylhexamethylene diisocyanate (TMHDI). Since thermoplastic melt processing methods such as injection molding are readily carried out at elevated temperatures, premature crosslinking due to sensitizer thermal instability is a significant processing concern. To overcome sensitizer thermal instability, free radical inhibitor can be added to provide thermal stabilization. However, free radical inhibitor can reduce the effectiveness of radiation crosslinking. In this study, we determined the inhibition effects of the inhibitor 1,4-benzoquinone (BQ) on thermal stabilization and radiation crosslinking of polyurethane SMPs solution blended with PETA. Sol/gel analysis of irradiated samples showed that free radical inhibitor at concentrations of 0-10,000 ppm had little to no inverse effects on gel fraction. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) showed a minor negative correlation between inhibitor composition and rubbery modulus. The study also showed inhibitor BQ was highly effective on the thermal stabilization of acrylic sensitizer PETA. The thermoplastic blends could be heated to 150 °C for up to 5 hours or to 125 °C for up to 24 hours if stabilized with 10,000 ppm BQ without undesired sensitizer reaction occurring. The blended samples could also be heated to 125 °C for up to 5 hours if stabilized with 1000 ppm BQ without reaction. We believe this study provides significant insight into methods for manipulation of the competing mechanisms of radiation crosslinking and thermal stabilization of radiation sensitizers, thereby facilitating further development of radiation crosslinkable thermoplastic SMPs.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Surfactant Removal from Single-Wall Carbon Nanotube Dispersions
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Until recently, the use of single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) in nanoelectronic devices has been limited due to the presence of both metallic and semiconducting SWCNT electronic-types. Advances in post-synthesis processing, using techniques such as column chromatography and density gradient ultracentrifugation (DGU), has allowed for successful SWCNT separation. Many separation techniques rely on the use of surfactants, commonly sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), to exploit differences in the surface chemistry or buoyant density of the SWCNTs, respectively. Therefore, complete surfactant removal from the SWCNT species is critical in order to fully probe the intrinsic physical and electrical properties of the electronic-type-separated SWCNTs. In the current study, an approach to surfactant removal is described whereby purification was systematically examined by employing a variety of acids, bases, and organic solvents. Upon mixing of the desired reagent, the SWCNT dispersions were bath sonicated, immersed in an ice bath, and observed over the course of 24 hours. Reagents were qualitatively deemed successful if they interrupted the SWCNT/surfactant interaction, yet did not change the solubility of the surfactant. Of those examined, five reagents yielded optimal results, including acetone, acetonitrile, N,N-dimethylacetamide, cyclohexylpyrrolidine, and ethanol. The SWCNTs were filtered into bulk papers, each containing 1 mg of SWCNT material, which was followed by thermal oxidation in air. Purification temperatures were determined based on the decomposition profile of the as-produced SWCNT paper obtained by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The purity of the treated SWCNT samples was characterized via Raman spectroscopy, optical absorbance spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and TGA. The use of organic reagents has led to a method for surfactant removal that also reduces filtration time, which may prove useful in large scale batch processing. Results demonstrating the successful removal of SDS from SWCNT dispersions will be discussed and compared to prevalent strategies previously reported in the literature.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: FORMATION OF A 3-D NETWORK IN ALGINATE SPHERES West Virginia University, Department of Chemical Engineering Paula Pacurari, Dr. Robin Hissam A current challenge in the study of cancer is the development of 3D models for cell growth. Growth of cells on flat surfaces may not allow for proper signaling or migration, yielding results that may not mimic the actual behavior of cancer cells in vivo. With a focus on leukemia, a material that will mimic the bone marrow microenvironment can serve as a new model for the study of leukemic stem cells. Alginate is an immunocompatible biopolymer that is capable of immobilizing viable cells and bioactive factors and is a common biological material used in drug delivery and biomaterial applications. Upon the addition of CaCl 2, alginate forms a hydrogel which can be modified into different 3-D structures. The bone marrow microenvironment is highly porous, and this project was to develop alginate structures that mimic the bone marrow microenvironment and can be used as a 3-D model. Alginate beads were formed using different solution concentrations to create materials of varying microstructures. Swelling ratio tests were performed to determine the porosity and diffusion rate of fluid into the material. In addition, the morphology of the beads was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were be used to characterize the structure of the 3-D networks. The bead structures were also compared to a bulk gel structure, which indicates the production of beads results in more porosity on the surface.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Analyzing ROS Generation From Magnetic Nanoparticles In An Alternating Magnetic Field and Its Role In Intracellular Hyperthermia
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Through Brownian relaxation and Neel relaxation, magnetic nanoparticles are capable of absorbing energy from an alternating magnetic field (AMF) and converting it to heat. Thus, via passive targeting, nanoparticles can collect at the tumor site and by the application of an AMF provide localized heating throughout the tumor. Furthermore, internalized targeted nanoparticles have been recently shown to induce cellular death when exposed to an AMF without a measurable temperature rise, therefore stimulating great interest to develop targeted nanoparticles for the treatment of metastatic cancer via intracellular hyperthermia. Focusing on the iron oxide magnetic nanoparticle system, it is thought that at the molecular level a significant contributing factor to the iron oxide toxicity in intracellular hyperthermia is the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) through the Fenton and Haber Weiss reactions. This research, in turn, focuses on the effects of an AMF on the surface mediated production of ROS based on the hypothesis that these effects are a key contributor to the toxicity demonstrated as intracellular hyperthermia. Despite variance in temperature ranging 37-39°C, it was observed via the methylene blue dye degradation method that samples exposed to an AMF experienced increased ROS production. Moreover, the Arrhenius equation , , where s -1 and J, was determined from a series of kinetic studies. This equation showed that despite variability in heating profile, experimental values of dye degradation were consistently lower than the theoretical values indicating improved kinetics due to AMF exposure. Furthermore, AMF data points did not fit the derived Arrhenius trendline strongly suggesting that AMF mediated heating possesses a kinetic effect unique to that of bulk heating. Preliminary cell culture studies conducted by means of the viability-ROS assay suggested that as uncoated iron oxide magnetic nanoparticle concentration increases, ROS generation increases and cell viability decreases.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Selective Patterning of Bi2Te3 Nanoplatelets Via Microcontact Printing
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Bismuth Telluride (Bi 2 Te 3 ) and its family chalcogenides are recently confirmed as topological insulators. Their electrical transport is dissipationless, which will have an impact on future applications, including thermoelectrics, electronics, and IR detectors. One of the critical challenges is to selectively assemble two-dimensional Bi 2 Te 3 nanosheets on a variety of substrates. In this work, the chemistry of selectively patterning Bi 2 Te 3 nanoplatelets on silicon substrates using micro contact printing (μCP) technique is investigated. Masters of three μCP stamps (patterns of letter A, houndstooth and square array, respectively) were made using regular photolithography processes, and μCP stamps were fabricated by pouring polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) on the master and curing PDMS at a temperature of 65⁰C for 3 hrs. μCP processes were applied to print 3-Aminopropyltrimethoxysilane (APTMS) with the three designed patterns onto silicon substrates, and Bi 2 Te 3 nanoplatelets, grown via a solvo-thermal process, were coated selectively. The results indicate that Bi 2 Te 3 nanoplatelets are immobilized on the APTMS printed regions. It is suspected that an electrostatic interaction between positively-charged amine groups and negatively-charged Bi 2 Te 3 nanoplatelets is the driving force of the selective patterning. We have demonstrated that μCP is a controllable, facile process for assembling two-dimensional Bi 2 Te 3 nanosheets and other chalcogenides.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Molecules containing cyanostilbene have attracted interest for their variable fluorescence properties attributable to its cis-trans isomerization. This molecule exhibits several characteristics that require further exploration. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: One cause of deafness is the loss of hair cells within the cochlea. This particular type of deafness can be partially remedied with a cochlear implant. Although these implants can reproduce the basic sensation of hearing, they deliver little tonal information due to poor spatial resolution. The distance between the transmitting electrode and the receiving hearing elements allows the signal to spread and electrically stimulate multiple regions of the nerve cells within the cochlea. One solution to deal with the poor spatial resolution may be to regenerate and guide spiral ganglion neurites to decrease the distance or even contact the electrode. Accordingly, we use photopolymerization to synthesize materials with surface physical and mechanical cues to orient the growth of regenerative neurites. Mechanical properties ware controlled by varying cross linking density in hexyl methyl methacrylate (HMA) with 1,6 hexanediol dimethacrylate (HDDMA) and polyethylene glycol dimethacrylate (PEGDMA) with ethylene glycol dimethacrylate (EGDMA) co-polymers. Each co-polymer system can be controlled by varying each components concentration to manipulate the elastic modulus while maintaining a relatively constant surface polarity.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Influence of Catalyst Deposition on Charge Carrier Trapping at Catalyst-Semiconductor Interfaces
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The production of solar fuels via photoelectrochemical water splitting is an attractive option for satisfying the world’s demand for clean energy. The success of this solar-to-chemical energy conversion depends highly on the identification of a stable and efficient photoanode for water oxidation. Bismuth vanadate (BiVO 4 ) is a promising photoanode material because of its small band gap, its stability over large pH ranges and favorable location of its valence band edge relative to the water oxidation potential. However, its surface is not catalytically active for water oxidation and its performance is limited. This problem can be mediated by the integration of an effective water oxidation catalyst such as cobalt phosphate (Co-Pi). Nevertheless, defects created at catalyst-semiconductor interfaces can lead to charge carrier trapping, preventing charge transfer to the catalyst and lowering conversion efficiency. This work provides a quantitative analysis of the accumulation of photogenerated holes at catalyst-semiconductor interfaces as a function of semiconductor doping and electrocatalyst deposition. In situ transient photocurrent and photovoltage behavior of a BiVO 4 photoanode coated with a Co-Pi electrocatalyst were measured in both a standard aqueous electrolyte and in one containing a sacrificial reagent. Associated time constants were analyzed to determine deleterious carrier trapping at these interfaces. Comparisons were also made with nominally undoped BiVO 4 , and molybdenum doped BiVO 4 with and without catalyst. Results presented here provide an important step to identifying parameters affecting the quality of BiVO 4 /Co-Pi interface and solidify a method of analyzing similar types of interfaces of importance to the development of artificial photosynthesis.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Time-Evolved Characterization and Performance of Slips (Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Surface) Tubing With Potential Drag Reduction
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: The development of energy-efficient, low-drag fluid transport systems would have a substantial impact on many promising industrial and commercial applications including fire-fighting operations, irrigation systems, pipeline transport, district heating systems, marine vessels, turbo machines, sports gear, and next-generation biomedical apparatus. The potential for traditional superhydrophobic surfaces to address this need is severely limited by high-pressure instability, a weakness that is exacerbated when subjected to low surface tension flow medium. Wong et al. have recently introduced Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Surfaces (SLIPS), a pressure-stable and truly omniphobic approach that promises to overcome these issues. Herein we rationally evaluate the viability of SLIPS as a means of drag reduction for fluid transport through metal pipes. We applied this functionalization, Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Inner Pipeline Extruded Surfaces (SLIPIPES), to 3 mm ID aluminum pipes, characterized the system for longevity and, and observed effects on pressure drop. We used water as a flow medium to assess longevity and compare friction factor of untreated aluminum (untreated-Al), boehmitized-fluorinated aluminum (BF-Al), and SLIPS aluminum tubing (SLIPS-Al) as a function time. First, to gauge the longevity of various lubricants, we studied the SLIPIPES as a function of time and Reynolds number, with the lubricant retention and resultant slip characteristics monitored by weight changes and sliding angle of a water droplet, respectively. The lubricant layer depletes over time at a rate proportional to the thickness and viscosity of the lubricant layer and the shear rate of the flowing medium. We observe a transition in thinning rate from the excess layer to the bound, ‘critical’ layer, and the lubricant layer is depleted after 30 minutes for nominal flow rates. Lastly, we observe no significant drag reduction in turbulent regime as the increasing drag caused by lubricant shedding outweighs the inner surface roughness improvement by SLIPS.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Integrated Opv-Otft System for Self-Powered, Solution Processable Organic Electronics
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Abstract: Integrated OPV-OTFT System for Self-Powered, Solution Processable Organic Electronics Renata Hanna, Doctor Yan Zhou, Professor Zhenan Bao Bao Group, Department of Chemical Engineering, Stanford University The field of organic electronics has attracted much attention from academia and industry for its flexible, light, low-cost, and solution processable devices. In recent years, efficient organic photovoltaics (OPVs), organic diodes (OLEDs), and organic transistors (OTFTs) have been studied and optimized. Going beyond the development of individual devices, in our study we propose a more complex circuit integrating OTFTs and OPVs. Transistors are widely employed as amplifiers and control units in current devices. In TFTs, the gate serves as a control and the channel is responsible for the amplified response. In OTFTs, the channel is a thin-film of organic semiconductors. Photovoltaics (PV) are a promising technology for attending global energy challenges. In PVs, the active layer is composed by an electron donor component and an electron acceptor component and is responsible for absorbing light and converting it into electricity. In OPVs, the active layer is a film composed of a blend of organic semiconductors. The integrated circuit (IC) we propose moves away from individual devices and towards fully organic, complex circuitry that can be processed on a single substrate without the need for lithography, a limiting factor in inorganic electronics. In the IC, OPV cells generate the voltage potential necessary to drive the OTFT in the saturation region, in which the transistor achieves best amplification conditions. The circuit structure developed is solution processable, and could be applied onto flexible substrates for specific applications. In this way, the IC proposed is a self-powered, solution processable, low-cost, and potentially flexible organic system. The proposed structure was developed with the intent to enable OPV characterization under solution environments, which is required for the study of many applications of the technology. Besides the original intent, further applications have also been devised for the proposed system. One simple application would be to apply it to flexible and portable devices that require low-weight and independent power generation. Another application would be to combine the already proposed structure to more OFET devices such as to create what are called current mirrors, through which it would be possible to amplify the current depending on the relations between device sizes. A further application of this structure would be as a type of photodetector for what is known as smart windows, which change coloration and the amount of light passing through depending on the intensity of the incident light. These applications would require further inquiry, but seem reasonable with further study, optimization, testing, and data collection. Another application that would have great market impact would be the use of this structure, coupled with other circuit elements, as an alternative form of radio-frequency identification (RFID) active transmitter. This configuration is advantageous over other forms of RFID transmitters for several reasons, and currently, the most apparent is that it is less costly in terms of materials and production methods, since organic electronics require cheap materials that can be processed without the high temperatures and vacuum levels that inorganic electronics require. The integrated circuit was prepared from solution through spin-coating techniques. The integration was achieved through a complex planning such that the production steps did not conflict with one another. This is important with the preparation of layers through spin-coating because the solution that is the precursor to a following layer cannot be able to dissolve previously formed layers. Moreover, it is important to have layer-planning such that the steps taken between layer- deposition steps , such as curing and annealing, do not conflict with the needs of other layers. The development of the correct sequence of layering and processing revealed the need for further study of the thickness of the dielectric layer. Optimization of the solvent and concentration of the dielectric solution was necessary for the formation of a clear solution and of a proper thin-film with reduced number of defects and pin-holes. Moreover, the study of the influence of the concentration over the thickness of the layer indicated a possible trade-off between high mobilities and low threshold voltages. Lower dielectric solution concentrations yielded thinner layers with higher mobilities (µ) and threshold voltages (V TH ), under the condition that the layers were thick enough to prevent shunting due to pin-holes. In opposition to these results, more concentrated solutions yielded lower mobilities and threshold voltages. Consequently, there is a need for compromising between high mobilities and low threshold voltage, both of which are desirable characteristics for the proposed IC. Low threshold voltages are essential so that the OPVs are capable of driving the OTFTs, whereas high mobilities are more desirable because they ensure better device performances. The study of polymer blends for the OPV active layer indicated the need for further optimization of the threshold voltage of the OTFTs since on average the OPVs could only drive up to approximately 0.9V. Considering the IC structure, higher driving voltages would allow better performances and amplification capabilities for the transistors. Therefore, although this study has achieved an efficient process for the preparation of the IC, much needs to be done in order for the system to be operational. The main points that continue to be studied are the optimization of the dielectric layer of the OTFT and of the active layer of the OPV.

The results illustrate that the doping, PLD target processing parameters, and substrate crystal orientation have the greatest impact on the ceria film surface characteristics.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Glucose-Initiated Accelerated Degradation of Poly (Beta-amino Ester) Hydrogels for Drug Delivery
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Hydrogels have long been used in the development of a range of applications such as intelligent drug delivery systems, tissue engineering, orthopedic implants, and other medical applications. Their three-dimensional structure, formed by crosslinking chains, allows them to absorb large quantities of water, thereby mimicking many soft tissues. Currently, there is a significant interest in intelligent drug delivery systems for the treatment of diabetes, and hydrogels could offer a unique platform for such applications provided they could sense and respond to glucose. For drug delivery, a hydrogel can be loaded with, and subsequently release, a drug in response to environmental stimuli. For degradable hydrogels, this response is the hydrolytic or enzymatic cleavage of chemical bonds resulting in erosion of the three-dimensional network. For biomedical applications, poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) is one of the most widely used polymers in hydrogels. Additionally, common PEG precursors can be combined with amines to form poly (b-amino ester) (PBAEs) hydrogels that are hydrolytically degradable as opposed to traditionally non-degradable PEG-based hydrogels. This project aims to investigate the rate of glucose-initiated degradation of hydrogels by measuring the mass loss ratio of the gels at different points of time. Macromers used for PBAE hydrogels were synthesized with a diacrylate:primary amine ratio of 1.2:1 using isobutylamine and varying ratios of PEG 400 diacrylate (PEG400DA) and diethylene glycol diacrylate (DEGDA). PBAE hydrogels with were synthesized by UV polymerization with 2,2 – dimethoxy-2-phenylacetophenone as a photoinitiator and DMSO as the solvent. The molar ratios of DEGDA:PEG400DA were varied at 1:1, 3:1 and 10:1 with the latter being the most hydrophobic and therefore displaying the longest degradation profile. Studies show that glucose and glucose oxidase reaction products are able to accelerate the degradation of PBAE hydrogels. The ability to accelerate the degradation of hydrogels by sensing glucose provides a platform for intelligent drug delivery systems composed of biocompatible materials with great potential for biomedical applications.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: While many natural features are rounded, few techniques exist to create microstructures with rounded features. Here, we describe an approach which uses microcontact printing to pattern molds around water and ice for the creation of 3D rounded microscale features. Microcontact printing is a technique that uses polymer stamps to create patterns of self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) in order to selectively modify the chemical properties of a surface. When these surfaces were exposed to water, the liquid localized on the hydrophilic regions of the pattern and could be frozen in place, forming arrays of curved, 3D structures. These patterned ice molds were then cast in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), forming polymer replicas of the three dimensional surfaces.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Piezoelectric and ferroelectric materials are useful as the active element in non-destructive monitoring devices for high-radiation environments. However, such use requires knowledge of the structural response in the material to radiation exposure, and the nature of these changes is not currently known. Thus, the present work evaluates the change in the structure of a variety of technologically significant lead zirconate titanate (PZT) compositions. PZT based materials with a 50/50 zirconium to titanium ratio of the following three compositions were investigated: (1) undoped, (2) Fe-doped, and (3) Nb-doped PZT. Powder samples and disc shaped samples of all three compositions were synthesized using solid state processing. Laboratory X-Ray diffraction was used to determine the initial phase purity of the materials. Half of all the samples were exposed to a 1 MeV equivalent fluence of 1.7×10 15 neutrons/cm 2 relative to the control group. After irradiation, neutron diffraction from the SMARTS diffractometer was used to analyze the crystal structures of each sample using Rietveld refinements. This approach allowed quantitative assessment of point defect concentrations. The refinements showed a mixture of the rhombohedral and tetragonal phases for these samples and most importantly showed that the oxygen and lead occupancies had measurably changed with irradiation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Discovery of ZnO-Binding Peptides for Photocatalytic Material Synthesis
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Clean air and water are important for sustainable habitats. Improved methods for maintaining and renewing these resources are critical. Photocatalysis is a promising technology for removal of toxic molecules and pollutants from air and water. Photocatalysis utilizes sunlight to activate photosensitive materials to catalyze chemical reactions necessary to degrade pollutants into innocuous compounds. Nanoscale zinc oxide (ZnO) displays optical and electrical properties suitable for photocatalysis. Furthermore, unlike other conventional methods, nanoscale biomineralized ZnO is advantageously manufactured under ambient conditions. The objective of this study was to find a specific peptide that binds to ZnO, with the possibility to biomineralize nanostructures of ZnO in the future. Biopanning, a combinatorial phage display technique with phages displaying approximately 10 7 different peptides, was used to select peptide sequences with affinity for ZnO. After five rounds of biopanning, two phages which showed strong affinity for ZnO were isolated. The peptides VPGAAEHT and DRQVDATA were displayed on these phages. To confirm the affinity of these phages for ZnO, binding tests were completed using a ZnO thin film grown on a silicon substrate as the target material. The identified phages, displaying VPGAAEHT and DRQVDATA peptides, were 79 and 61 times more likely to bind to the ZnO thin film on a silicon substrate target than the wild-type control phage, respectively. Binding studies were also performed using the silicon substrate as a target to ensure the phage affinity was for the ZnO thin film rather than the silicon substrate. The VPGAAEHT phage demonstrated an affinity for the ZnO thin film which was more than twice that observed for the silicon substrate alone, whereas the DRQVDATA phage showed a comparable affinity for both the ZnO thin film and the silicon substrate. These results will benefit future research to biomineralized nanostructured ZnO material which could be used for photocatalytic devices.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Dynamic Contact Angles in Splashing
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Samantha Jones, Andrzej Latka, and Sidney R. Nagel When a drop of liquid impacts a solid surface it will splash emitting tiny droplets. This phenomenon results from a variety of complex interactions between the liquid and the substrate. Surprisingly, when air pressure is reduced splashing is completely suppressed [1-3]. The mechanism by which air induces splashing is still unexplained and the question remains: where does the air matter? In this project we consider the air at the advancing edge of the spreading drop. This was done by studying the dynamic contact angle between the spreading liquid and the solid surface. Using high-speed videos of drop impacts, we measured the evolution of the dynamic contact angle for water/glycerol drops of different viscosities. We found that the contact angle increases as the edge of the drop decelerates. At late times, the liquid shows a pronounced overturning, that is the contact angle grows to be significantly greater than 90°, so that the spreading liquid is more likely to engulf air as it moves. This behavior was robust and was unaffected by the viscosity of the liquid. [1] L. Xu, W.W. Zhang, and S.R. Nagel, Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 184505 (2005) [2] M. M. Driscoll, C.S. Stevens, and S.R. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: The Effect of Surface Coating on Magnetic Properties and Local Structure in Coated Cobalt Nanoparticles
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Magnetic cobalt nanoparticles have potential applications in magnetic data storage devices. They can be arranged densely enough on a substrate to eclipse current data storage methods. At temperatures below the blocking temperature (Tb), these nanoparticles can retain the direction of their magnetic moment even when an applied magnetic field is removed. The direction of each nanoparticle’s magnetic moment corresponds to one bit of information. One challenge to developing these materials is that the Tb for small cobalt nanoparticles is below 10K. One way to increase the Tb is by increasing the surface anisotropy of the nanoparticle with a surface coating. To study this effect, one sample of cobalt nanoparticles was oxidized, forming a CoO shell while another was coated with silicon dioxide to prevent oxidation and serve as a reference to the oxidized sample. The resulting blocking temperatures and local structures were studied. Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the presence of spherical nanoparticles and was used to determine the size distribution. Synchrotron x-ray pair distribution function (PDF) analysis was used to study the effects of coating on the local structure of nanoparticles. The blocking temperature and oxidation state were determined from MPMS magnetometer data. The PDF of the silica coated nanoparticles shows a hexagonal structure, with different lattice constants than the bulk phase. The PDF of the Co/CoO core shell nanoparticles indicates a distorted cubic structure and a large amount of CoO. The magnetization data reveal a Tb of 5K for the silica coated nanoparticles and no trace of oxidation, in contrast to the CoO nanoparticles, where the Tb was 250K.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Title: The Effect of Bucky-Ball Nanoparticle Additives on the Electrowetting-on-Dielectric Response of Two Ionic Liquids Abstract for Poster Presentation at the 2013 AIChE Annual Student Conference, November 1-5, San Francisco, California Authors: Glenn R. Hafenstine†, Marriner H. Merrill*‡, and James P. Thomas‡ †Chemical Engineering Department; Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506, USA ‡Multifunctional Materials Branch, Code 6350; Naval Research Laboratory (NRL), Washington, DC 20375, USA *Corresponding Author: marriner.merrill@nrl.navy.mil Abstract: Electrowetting-on-Dielectric (EWOD) is an effective method for manipulating small volumes of liquids in applications such as lab-on-a-chip systems, e-microreactors, and novel multifunctional materials. EWOD uses an applied electrical potential between a drop of conductive liquid and a dielectric-coated electrode (on a solid substrate) to effect changes in the liquid-solid contact angle. As the potential is applied, it tends to “spread” the drop out over the drop-substrate interface regions that are electroded, decreasing the contact angle. Ionic liquids are often used in EWOD applications due to their low vapor pressures (non-evaporating) and their wide range of available chemistries. In this work, we evaluate the effect of adding nanoparticles (diameters ranging from 1 to 100’s nm) on the EWOD response (contact angle change with applied potential) for several ionic liquids over a 0 to +/- 200 V applied potential range. Previous research on a dispersion of 7.7 nm quantum dots in an aqueous solvent reported significantly enhanced EWOD response over that predicted by the Lippmann-Young equation. Of the various nanoparticle-IL’s tested in our work, the 0.05 wt% solution of 0.71-nm ‘bucky-balls’ in 1-Butyl-2,3-dimethylimidazolium nitrate (MMBI-NO 3 ) showed the best improvement in EWOD response (23% decrease in actuating voltage for the same contact angle change). The same nanoparticles added to 1-Ethyl-3-methylimidazolium methyl sulfate (MEI-MeSO 4 ), however, showed only slight improvement in EWOD response. At this stage of the research, we do not fully understand the role played by the bucky-ball additives in improving EWOD response with the MMBI-NO 3 nor the reason no improvement in response was observed with the bucky-ball additives in MEI-MeSO 4 . Ion chemistry, and nanoparticle dispersion quality and segregation within the droplet are potential mechanisms being investigated. Further testing with several different ionic liquids of varied cations and anions is being conducted to answer these questions.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Thermoelectric Power Generation in Dynamic Temperature Environments
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Thermoelectric materials have long held promise as a critical piece of the sustainable-energy puzzle. The benefits of thermoelectric power are numerous: they capture energy from waste heat (such as that of industrial processes and automobile exhaust) and naturally-occurring thermal gradients (such as geothermal energy), have a small size, degrade slowly, generally consist of nontoxic materials, and operate silently; however, their widespread adaptation has been limited by their low power outputs and efficiencies. Although a large number of thermoelectric applications have been considered, investigated, and commercialized, the thermal driving force remains the same in each: a steady-state, spatial temperature gradient. Here, an alternate source of thermal energy for thermoelectric power – transient thermal gradients, or the fluctuations of an environmental temperature with time – is investigated; this source of power is useful for low-power devices in remote locations. We design and characterize devices that employ a thermoelectric module sandwiched between two heat exchangers with significantly different thermal masses and examine the effects of heat exchanger size and material selection, period of oscillation of the environmental temperature fluctuations, and radiative heat transfer on the thermoelectric power output. We report maximum experimental power generation on the order of milliwatts using standard bismuth telluride thermoelectric modules in devices with a size of about 10 cm 3 .

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.title: Improving Nanoparticle Biocompatibility through Graphene Encapsulation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2013/webp.abstract: Biocompatibility is required when materials are introduced to biological systems. We have synthesized binary systems of silver nanoparticles encapsulated by reduced graphene oxide sheets (nanosacks) that may improve biocompatibility. The effect nanoparticles have on reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in a biological system is important to consider because ROS, such as hydroxyl radicals, can be toxic and lead to cell damage. To learn if graphene encapsulation can reduce nanoparticle toxicity, citrate coated silver nanoparticles are applied as a model system for studying nanosack properties. Hydroxyl radical production in pure silver nanoparticles is compared with hydroxyl radical production in encapsulated silver by monitoring the degradation of Rhodamine B. Our early results show that the nanosacks appear to slow hydroxyl radical production. In the presence of hydrogen peroxide, silver nanoparticles display the fastest decoloration of dye while silver filled nanosacks degrade dye at slower rates.
